If the lot/stock inconsistency is persistent (it requires an inventarizatsiya to fix), the record is retried by every syncTick (30 s), online event, login, and submitSale — each retry executes the whole _create_sale_once transaction server-side (inventory FOR UPDATE locks in global order, doc_seq counter lock, 3x IntegrityError retries) before failing again. There is no retry counter, exponential backoff, aging, or operator alert; the cashier just sees a pending badge that never clears, and the periodic lock traffic degrades concurrent checkout on the same products.
findings.invariant: A record that has failed identically N times must escalate to a human-visible state instead of hammering the same locking transaction forever.
findings.attack_scenario: One offline receipt for a tracked product hits the stock/lot invariant (409 LOT_INVARIANT_BROKEN) after a bad receiving correction. For days, every POS tick re-locks the busiest product's inventory row and receipt counter, slowing live sales, while the money-captured receipt sits in 'pending' with no path to resolution short of a developer clearing localStorage.
findings.evidence: sync.ts: `else if (r.retry) { /* outbox'da SAQLAYMIZ, keyingi flush qayta uradi */ }` with startSync `setInterval(..., 30000)`; sales.py lot gate: `raise HTTPException(409, "Savdoni yozib bo'lmadi — partiya va qoldiq mos kelmadi...", headers=EC.headers(EC.LOT_INVARIANT_BROKEN))` and the comment '409 QOLADI: /sync/push uni tranzient deb biladi'.

verdicts.reasoning: The mechanical claims are accurate as code facts: apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py push() sets `_transient = e.status_code >= 500 or e.status_code == 409` (retry:true for every 409), and packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts flushOutbox keeps a `r.retry` record in the outbox with no counter, backoff, aging, or cap, retried by a 30 s setInterval. But the finding's premise — a PERSISTENT 409 reachable through the app — does not survive reading the code. (1) The named trigger is unreachable: a "bad receiving correction" cannot commit lot/stock drift, because the correction itself runs the same pre-commit gate (apps/server/app/services/lot_correction.py:1195 `SI.assert_ok` -> rollback -> 409). Every lot-touching writer is gated before commit: sales (services/sales.py:709), writeoff (api/v1/inventory.py:284), stock count (inventory.py:595), receiving (services/lot_receiving.py:320, api/v1/receiving.py:474), returns (api/v1/sales.py:1106), track_lots enable (api/v1/lots.py:325), shortfall resolution (services/lot_resolution.py:449). A committed state violating the invariant therefore cannot be produced by the application; the tests that exercise LOT_INVARIANT_BROKEN (tests/test_lot_safe_409.py) have to corrupt the DB directly (`_buzish`). (2) The offline replay path (/sync/push always calls create_sale with honor_price_snapshot=True) is specifically engineered so no OTHER persistent 409 exists either: the stock guard is bypassed (QA WH-007, services/sales.py — negative stock allowed), FEFO valid-lot shortage does NOT 409 on replay but writes a LotShortfall debt row (the invariant is two-term: Inventory.qty == SUM(lots) - open shortfalls, so the gate still passes), and the price-drift 409 "Narxlar yangilandi" is `if not honor_price_snapshot` only. Genuinely permanent business errors (no open shift, bad terminal, invalid till, discount cap, Numeric overflow) are 400s and DO dead-letter with a stable X-Error-Code, giving the human-visible "N rad etildi" state the invariant demands. (3) Even in the out-of-band-corruption case, the record is not unrecoverable-by-developer-only: the finding itself concedes an inventarizatsiya fixes it, and that count endpoint (inventory.py stock count with lot decrements/surpluses) restores the invariant, after which the next 30 s flush replays the sale successfully (recording a shortfall if needed) — no localStorage surgery required. Meanwhile every online sale/writeoff/count of the drifted product fails loudly fail-closed and the server writes log.exception with LOT_INVARIANT_BROKEN on each attempt, so the state is operator-visible, and the POS shows a persistent pending badge. (4) The load claim is not credible: one short rolled-back transaction per 30 s per queued record (flushOutbox is single-flight via the `flushing` flag) is negligible lock traffic. The retry-forever-for-409 choice is a deliberate, tested financial-safety trade-off (services/sales.py:724 "409 QOLADI ... pul olingan offline chek outbox'dan TUSHIB QOLMAYDI"; tests/test_lot_safe_409.py::test_OFFLINE_replay_darvozada_TRANZIENT_qoladi_va_KOD_beradi): dead-lettering a money-captured receipt on a state that is either transient or fixable by a standard count would be the actual lost-sale defect.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Universal pre-commit stock_invariant.assert_ok gate on every lot-mutating writer — including lot_correction.py (the finding's alleged trigger), so committed lot/stock drift is unreachable through the application — combined with the replay-only bypasses in services/sales.py (stock-guard bypass QA WH-007, LotShortfall debt ledger instead of the online FEFO 409, honored price snapshot) that remove every other application-reachable persistent 409; permanent business failures use 400 + X-Error-Code and are dead-lettered to the visible "N rad etildi" state; the inventarizatsiya endpoint (api/v1/inventory.py stock count) is a built-in operator path that repairs drift and unblocks the queued record.
verdicts.repro_hint: To demonstrate the residual (out-of-scope) behavior one must corrupt the DB out-of-band: UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 for a tracked product (as tests/test_lot_safe_409.py `_buzish` does), queue an offline sale, and observe /sync/push return retry:true each 30 s tick; then run a stock count for that product and observe the next flush drain the record — showing the stuck state is operator-recoverable, not developer-only.

findings.title: Online sale can commit into an already-closed shift, excluded from frozen expected_cash (sale-vs-close TOCTOU)
findings.claim: The online sale path reads the cashier's open Shift without any lock or later status re-check (services/sales.py:104-110), while close_shift locks the Shift FOR UPDATE (api/v1/shifts.py:540), computes the frozen expected_cash, and commits. A sale whose Shift SELECT ran before close acquired the lock, but whose first flush (INSERT sales, sales.py:240-241) ran after, merely blocks on the FK KEY SHARE vs FOR UPDATE conflict, then proceeds after close commits: it attaches Sale.shift_id to the now-CLOSED shift and its cash payment is missing from the frozen s.expected_cash.
findings.invariant: Every cash sale attributed to a shift must be included in that shift's frozen expected_cash (Z-report), or be rejected/redirected; a closed shift's report must equal the sum of its attributed cash sales.
findings.attack_scenario: Cashier taps 'close shift' on one terminal while a sale request is in flight: (1) sale tx reads Shift (status=open, no lock) at sales.py:105; (2) close tx locks Shift FOR UPDATE, computes expected (legacy SalePayment sum or ledger_expected_shift_cash), dual-writes recon, commits; (3) sale tx's db.flush() at sales.py:241 was blocked on the FK row lock, now proceeds, inserts Sale with shift_id of the closed shift, posts its cash ledger leg as OFF_SHIFT/LATE_SYNC (cash.shift already closed), and commits. Result: Z-report difference is wrong by the sale amount (phantom surplus in the drawer), Sale permanently reports under a closed shift, and the ledger leg sits outside the frozen reconciliation. QA SHIFT-1 fixed this TOCTOU for add_cash_movement/cash_op/refund by locking the Shift row, but the sale path was never given the same lock or a post-flush status re-check.
findings.evidence: sales.py:104-110 `db.query(Shift).filter(Shift.cashier_id == emp.id, Shift.status == ShiftStatus.open).first()` — no with_for_update, no re-check after the blocking flush at :241. shifts.py:534-538 comment lists add_cash_movement/cash_op/cash-refund as the serialized writers ('hammasi smenani qulflaydi') — sales is absent from that list. FK Sale.shift_id -> shifts.id (models/sales.py:25-27) only makes the INSERT wait; it does not invalidate the stale in-memory shift object, and reject_closed_shift_replay in require_post_t0_till reads that stale object (status still 'open').
findings.suggested_repro: PG, two sessions: S1 begin; run sale flow up to the Shift SELECT and pause before db.add(sale). S2: POST /shifts/{id}/close, commit. Resume S1: INSERT sales succeeds; assert sale.shift_id == closed shift id and sale cash amount not in shifts.expected_cash.

verdicts.reasoning: The broken path is provable by reading the code at 482b3f38. (1) apps/server/app/services/sales.py::_create_sale_once reads the cashier's open Shift with a plain `db.query(Shift)...filter(status == open).first()` — no with_for_update, and no status re-check at any point after the first `db.flush()` (the only later gates are the lot/stock invariant); the only FOR UPDATE locks in the sale path are Inventory, QrPayment and Customer. (2) apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py::close_shift locks the Shift FOR UPDATE, computes expected_cash (legacy SalePayment sum, or ledger_expected_shift_cash override) and freezes it; its own QA SHIFT-1 comment enumerates the serialized writers — add_cash_movement/cash_op/cash-refund — and the sale path is absent from that list. (3) The interleaving is exactly as claimed: if close acquires the FOR UPDATE after the sale's unlocked Shift SELECT but before the sale's first flush, the sale's `INSERT INTO sales` merely blocks on the FK's FOR KEY SHARE vs FOR UPDATE conflict, resumes after close commits (FK only needs the row to exist, not to be open), and commits Sale.shift_id pointing at the now-CLOSED shift, whose expected_cash was frozen without it — phantom surplus at Z-report. No protective mechanism rejects or redirects it: (a) cutover_guard.require_post_t0_till → reject_closed_shift_replay runs BEFORE the insert on the stale in-memory shift object and is inert for pre-T0 tenants (enforcement_active false), so it cannot see a close committing inside the window; (b) the ledger layer explicitly anticipates this race — posting.py::_lock_candidate_shift is commented "(sale-vs-close)" and _resolve_shift says "CLOSED (yoki CLOSING — lock ostida CLOSED bo'lib qoladi)" — but its remedy is to RECORD the leg as LATE_SYNC/LATE_SYNC_UNACK (Case C) or OFF_SHIFT/UNRESOLVED_OFF_SHIFT (Case D, when retrofit._open_cash_shift_id already sees the closed cash.shift), never to abort the sale or repair the frozen legacy expected_cash; (c) cash_ddl_v1.sql triggers are immutability guards only — nothing constrains sales.shift_id against shift status. One important narrowing correction to the finding: once the sale HAS flushed its INSERT (holding FOR KEY SHARE on the shifts row), close_shift's FOR UPDATE blocks behind it until the sale commits and close then includes it — so the FK is a partial protective constraint that confines the race to the window between the Shift SELECT and the first db.flush(); but that window contains the force_shift settings query, terminal/till resolution and both cutover-guard calls (multiple round-trips), so it is concretely exploitable by "close tapped while a sale request is in flight". The invariant violation (sale attributed to a closed shift and excluded from its frozen expected_cash in both legacy and ledger-native modes) follows deterministically from standard Postgres READ COMMITTED + row-lock semantics; the LATE_SYNC machinery's existence is the authors' own acknowledgement that the leg can land post-close, with no corresponding fix on the legacy attribution/Z side.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial only: (1) FK sales.shift_id -> shifts.id makes any sale that has already flushed its INSERT hold FOR KEY SHARE on the Shift row, so close_shift's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE blocks until that sale commits and its payment IS included in expected_cash — this narrows the race to the pre-first-flush window but does not close it. (2) posting.py::_lock_candidate_shift + _resolve_shift ("sale-vs-close" comment) lock the cash.shift row and, seeing it CLOSED under lock, downgrade the ledger leg to LATE_SYNC/OFF_SHIFT with an anomaly flag — protecting ledger classification/recon integrity, but recording rather than rejecting, and leaving Sale.shift_id and the frozen shifts.expected_cash wrong. (3) reject_closed_shift_replay exists but runs pre-insert on the stale in-memory shift and only for post-T0 tenants. No unique index, trigger, or post-flush re-check protects the legacy attribution.
verdicts.repro_hint: PG, two sessions, one cashier with an open shift. S1: begin the sale request and pause it between the Shift SELECT (services/sales.py, the `Shift.status == open` query in _create_sale_once) and the first `db.flush()` after `db.add(sale)` (e.g. breakpoint, or artificially slow the force_shift Settings query). S2: POST /shifts/{id}/close with counted_cash including the in-flight sale's cash; let it commit. Resume S1 to completion (expect 200). Assert: sale.shift_id == closed shift id; shifts.expected_cash excludes the sale's SalePayment amount, so difference shows a phantom surplus equal to the sale; in a ledger-native tenant additionally assert the cash_ledger_entries row for the sale has posting_kind LATE_SYNC or OFF_SHIFT (not ON_SHIFT) and an LATE_SYNC_UNACK/UNRESOLVED_OFF_SHIFT exception, while the reconciliation_records snapshot frozen at close also excludes it.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not — every candidate protection fails on inspection of SHA 482b3f38.

1) The unlocked read is real and never revisited. apps/server/app/services/sales.py `_create_sale_once` selects the shift with `db.query(Shift).filter(Shift.cashier_id == emp.id, Shift.status == ShiftStatus.open).first()` — no with_for_update. I read the entire function through `db.commit()`: after this SELECT the Shift is never re-queried, refreshed, or status-checked again. The session is `autoflush=False, expire_on_commit=False` (apps/server/app/db/session.py:72), so nothing invalidates the stale in-memory object.

2) close_shift (apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py) takes `db.query(Shift).filter(Shift.id == shift_id).with_for_update().first()` — full FOR UPDATE — then computes frozen expected_cash from committed SalePayment rows (or `ledger_expected_shift_cash`, which for a ledger-native tenant reads ON_SHIFT ledger legs), sets status=closed, commits. Its own QA SHIFT-1 comment enumerates the serialized writers: "add_cash_movement/cash_op/cash-refund (hammasi smenani qulflaydi)" — the sale path is conspicuously absent from that list, and indeed sales.py contains no Shift lock.

3) The FK is not a guard. models/sales.py:25-27 `shift_id ... ForeignKey("shifts.id")` — the RI check on the sale's first `db.flush()` (right after `db.add(sale)`) takes FOR KEY SHARE on the shifts row, which conflicts with close's FOR UPDATE, so the flush merely WAITS until close commits, then succeeds (the row still exists). Blocking is not even required for the bug: under READ COMMITTED, close's SalePayment sum cannot see the sale's uncommitted rows, so any sale that read the shift before close's lock but commits after close's snapshot produces the same outcome. The window between the shift SELECT and the first flush spans dozens of statements (settings, terminal, till validation, cutover guards, product loads) — trivially hittable with two concurrent requests (sync endpoints, per-request sessions).

4) The only status re-check on the sale path, `reject_closed_shift_replay` (services/cash/cutover_guard.py:207-224, called from `require_post_t0_till`:318), (a) runs BEFORE `db.add(sale)`, (b) reads `getattr(shift, "status")` off the stale in-memory ORM object which still says 'open', and (c) is gated on `cash_enabled` + `enforcement_active` — for a legacy/pre-T0 tenant there is no check at all.

5) The ledger side does not raise. After close committed, `on_cash_sale` (services/cash/retrofit.py:228-248) calls `_open_cash_shift_id` → `repo.open_shift_for_account` finds no OPEN cash.shift → passes `origin_shift_id=None`; `_resolve_shift` (services/cash/posting.py:321-340) hits Case D and returns OFF_SHIFT + ["UNRESOLVED_OFF_SHIFT"] — an anomaly flag, not an error. The sale then commits normally. (Minor correction to the finding: the leg is OFF_SHIFT/Case D, not LATE_SYNC — LATE_SYNC requires origin_shift_id to name the closed shift, but resolution here returns None.)

6) No DB trigger or CHECK protects shifts/sales — the cash-schema triggers (cash_ddl_v1.sql) only enforce ledger immutability.

Net result, provable by reading alone: Sale.shift_id points at a shift whose status=closed and whose frozen expected_cash/reconciliation excludes this sale's cash, while the physical cash IS in the drawer (phantom surplus in Z-report difference), violating the invariant "every cash sale attributed to a shift is included in that shift's frozen expected_cash". The existing FOR UPDATE only protects the opposite interleaving (sale flushed first → close waits → sees it).
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. The FK sales.shift_id→shifts.id only delays the INSERT (FOR KEY SHARE waits on close's FOR UPDATE, then succeeds); reject_closed_shift_replay reads the stale pre-lock ORM object and runs before the first flush; the ledger posting engine classifies the post-close leg as OFF_SHIFT (Case D) instead of rejecting; no trigger/CHECK exists on shifts/sales.
verdicts.repro_hint: PG, two sessions on one cashier's open shift. S1 (sale): execute _create_sale_once up to but not past `db.add(sale); db.flush()` (e.g. breakpoint after the Shift SELECT in services/sales.py). S2: POST /shifts/{id}/close with counted_cash — commits, freezing expected_cash. Resume S1 to completion. Assert: sale.shift_id == closed shift id; shifts.expected_cash excludes the sale's cash SalePayment; for a ledger-native tenant the cash_ledger_entries row for the sale has posting_kind='OFF_SHIFT' with anomaly UNRESOLVED_OFF_SHIFT.

findings.title: sync.push bare `except Exception` permanently dead-letters paid offline sales on transient DB errors that are not OperationalError
findings.claim: Per-record triage treats only HTTPException(409/5xx) and sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError as transient (sync.py:65-80). Any other transient failure — sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError ('connection already closed' mid-statement), generic DBAPIError disconnect wraps, or a Python-level race — falls into the bare `except Exception` (sync.py:81-88) and returns ok:false with no retry flag, so the client (flushOutbox, packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts:188-192) moves the money-already-taken receipt to the dead-letter list and removes it from the outbox.
findings.invariant: A paid offline receipt may only leave the retry queue for a deterministic business rejection; infrastructure failures must keep it queued (the QA OFF-1 'no lost transactions' rule).
findings.attack_scenario: Railway Postgres restarts (or the pooled connection is severed) exactly while /sync/push is processing record N. psycopg2 raises InterfaceError instead of OperationalError; the bare handler rolls back and answers {ok:false, retry:absent}. The client dead-letters the receipt: sale, stock movement and cash leg are never written, and the only trace is the failed-list JSON that the cashier can two-step clear. The sale must be manually re-rung to recover.
findings.evidence: sync.py:77-80 catches OperationalError -> retry:true; sync.py:81-88 `except Exception: ... results.append({... "ok": False, "error": "server"})` with no `retry` key. In SQLAlchemy, InterfaceError and DBAPIError are siblings of OperationalError, not subclasses, so a dropped-connection InterfaceError bypasses the transient branch. Client: sync.ts flushOutbox `else if (r.retry) keep; else deadLetter(...) && outboxRemove(...)`.
findings.suggested_repro: Monkeypatch create_sale to raise sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError once; POST /sync/push with one receipt; assert result has ok:false and no retry:true, i.e. the client contract dead-letters it.

verdicts.reasoning: The code structure is as claimed: apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py push() marks only HTTPException 409/5xx and sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError as retry:true; the bare `except Exception` returns ok:false with no retry key, and packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts flushOutbox() then dead-letters the receipt and removes it from the outbox (visible in the failed list, but no automatic retry — the OFF-1 invariant is broken for any such error). HOWEVER, the finding's headline attack is REFUTED: the server uses psycopg v3, not psycopg2 (apps/server/app/db/session.py::_normalize rewrites to "postgresql+psycopg://"). In psycopg 3, connection-loss errors ("the connection is closed", "server closed the connection unexpectedly", SSL failures) are psycopg.OperationalError — psycopg3 deliberately moved closed-connection errors out of InterfaceError — so SQLAlchemy raises sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError and the Railway-restart-mid-statement scenario lands in the retry:true branch. Further protections: pool_pre_ping=True + pool_recycle=1800 recycle stale connections at checkout; create_sale (apps/server/app/services/sales.py:43-50) retries IntegrityError 3x and converts it to HTTPException(409) → retry:true, covering receipt_no/inventory races; post-commit refresh/notify failures are swallowed (QA OFF-8, sales.py:737-746). What survives and keeps this PLAUSIBLE rather than REFUTED: sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError (QueuePool checkout timeout, pool_timeout=30) is a SQLAlchemyError that is NOT an OperationalError subclass and NOT an HTTPException. Because _create_sale_once commits per record (sales.py:737), the session releases and re-acquires a pool connection for every record in the push loop; under pool exhaustion — a scenario the engine config comment in session.py itself documents as occurring under production concurrency, and most likely during the post-outage thundering-herd flush — a mid-loop checkout raises TimeoutError into the bare except, and the paid offline receipt is permanently dead-lettered. The broken code path is statically provable; only the runtime occurrence of TimeoutError mid-loop (rather than at the auth dependency, where the whole-request failure is handled safely by the client) requires a test. Severity should be downgraded from P1: the common disconnect/restart vectors are all handled, the surviving window is narrow, and the dead-letter is visible to the cashier (not silent loss), though recovery requires manual re-ringing.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: 1) Driver is psycopg v3 (session.py _normalize forces postgresql+psycopg://): connection-loss errors surface as sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError → retry:true, refuting the claimed InterfaceError vector. 2) pool_pre_ping=True + pool_recycle=1800 recycle dead/stale connections at checkout. 3) create_sale's 3-attempt IntegrityError wrap converts write races to HTTPException(409) → retry:true. 4) Post-commit refresh/notify exceptions are swallowed (QA OFF-8), preventing false permanent rejects of committed sales. 5) Client-side: deadLetter() must succeed (returns true) before outboxRemove, and whole-request failures never dead-letter. No mechanism covers sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError (pool checkout timeout) raised mid-loop — that transient still reaches the bare except with no retry flag.
verdicts.repro_hint: In a server test (SQLite is fine), monkeypatch app.api.v1.sync.create_sale (or the Session's connection acquisition) to raise sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError("QueuePool limit reached") on the first call, then POST /sync/push with one valid receipt carrying a client_uuid. Assert the per-record result is {ok: false, error: "server"} with no "retry" key. Per the client contract in packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts flushOutbox() (else-branch: deadLetter + outboxRemove), that response removes the paid receipt from the retry queue. For completeness, also raise sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError in the same harness and assert retry:true, demonstrating the asymmetry between two equally transient infrastructure errors.

verdicts.reasoning:
The code shape the finding describes is real: in apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py `push`, the bare `except Exception` appends `{"ok": False, "error": "server"}` with no `retry` key, and packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts `flushOutbox` dead-letters and outbox-removes any ok:false result lacking retry:true. But the attack cannot be made concrete because no realistic transient failure reaches that handler in this runtime:

1. Wrong driver premise. The engine is psycopg v3, not psycopg2: apps/server/app/db/session.py `_normalize` rewrites the URL to `postgresql+psycopg://`, and apps/server/requirements.txt pins `psycopg[binary]>=3.2` (no psycopg2 anywhere in the app). The finding's InterfaceError scenario is psycopg2 folklore.

2. psycopg3's exception taxonomy funnels essentially every infrastructure failure into OperationalError, which sync.py catches (`except OperationalError` -> retry:true). Per psycopg3's documented SQLSTATE-class mapping, classes 08 (connection_exception), 40 (deadlock/serialization), 53 (insufficient_resources), 55 (lock_not_available), 57 (query_canceled, AdminShutdown 57P01 — the exact "Railway Postgres restarts" case), and 58 (system errors) all inherit psycopg.OperationalError. Client-side disconnects mid-statement ("server closed the connection unexpectedly", "consuming input failed") and use of a closed connection (psycopg3 `_check_connection_ok` raises OperationalError("the connection is closed"), not InterfaceError — psycopg3 reserves InterfaceError for API misuse like a closed cursor) are OperationalError too. SQLAlchemy wraps a DBAPI error as the same-named sqlalchemy.exc class, so all of these arrive as sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError. Connect-phase failures at pool checkout are likewise wrapped as sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError via SQLAlchemy's no-connection error handling, and `pool_pre_ping=True` (session.py) transparently replaces stale pooled connections, closing the between-requests window.

3. The other transient classes are already triaged as retry: unique-constraint races go through create_sale's 3x IntegrityError retry loop (apps/server/app/services/sales.py:43-49) ending in HTTPException(409) -> retry:true; the lot-invariant gate raises 409 explicitly to stay transient (sales.py ~726); post-commit refresh failures are swallowed so the already-written sale still returns ok:true (QA OFF-8, sales.py ~744).

4. If the session is broken badly enough that `db.rollback()` inside a handler itself raises, the exception escapes the whole endpoint as a 500 — and the client's chunk-level catch in flushOutbox ("BUTUN so'rov xatosi") keeps the entire chunk queued, never dead-letters.

The one residual class that would dead-letter is sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError on pool checkout, but at the audited config it is not reachable: pool_size 15 + max_overflow 25 = 40 connections, while FastAPI's sync-endpoint threadpool caps at 40 concurrent request workers each holding at most one connection, so checkout exhaustion cannot occur without operator env overrides. The bare except's actual population is what its comment says: deterministic permanent errors (DataError/Numeric overflow, code bugs), for which dead-lettering is the intended contract.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: psycopg v3 driver (requirements.txt `psycopg[binary]>=3.2`; session.py `_normalize` -> postgresql+psycopg://): its SQLSTATE mapping makes every realistic transient failure (connection loss incl. server restart/AdminShutdown, deadlock, serialization, lock/statement timeout, resource exhaustion, closed-connection reuse) a psycopg.OperationalError, which SQLAlchemy surfaces as sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError — caught by sync.py's retry:true branch. Plus pool_pre_ping=True for stale connections, create_sale's IntegrityError->409 retry wrapper, and the client's whole-request catch that keeps the chunk queued on any endpoint-level 500.
verdicts.repro_hint: To confirm the refutation empirically (Postgres, psycopg3): kill the backend pid via pg_terminate_backend while /sync/push is mid-create_sale and assert the result is {ok:false, retry:true} (sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError wrapping psycopg.errors.AdminShutdown/ConnectionFailure). The only way to force the dead-letter path with a transient is to monkeypatch create_sale to raise sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError or InterfaceError directly — classes the real driver does not emit for disconnects — which demonstrates the gap is theoretical, not reachable. Optional hardening, not P1: also catch sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError with connection_invalidated plus TimeoutError as retry:true.

findings.title: on_cash_collection / on_bank_deposit gate on cash_enabled, not dual_write_enabled — they keep writing (or hard-failing) in LEGACY_ONLY mode
findings.claim: Every other posting hook is guarded by dual_write_enabled(db) (cash_enabled AND mode != LEGACY_ONLY), but on_cash_collection (retrofit.py:443-460) and on_bank_deposit check only `cash_enabled(db)`. With SAVDOOS_CASH_MODE=LEGACY_ONLY (the documented emergency 'ledger vaqtincha o'chirilsa' state, services/cash/mode.py), collections still attempt TILL->SAFE transfer legs into the supposedly-frozen ledger.
findings.invariant: LEGACY_ONLY means no ledger writes at all; all dual-write hooks must no-op uniformly so the ledger stays a consistent frozen snapshot.
findings.attack_scenario: Operator flips the mode to LEGACY_ONLY after a ledger incident. Sales and payins stop writing IN legs, so the TILL's ledger balance freezes; a cashier then runs a collection: post_transfer's OUT-sufficiency check reads the stale frozen balance and either (a) rejects with INSUFFICIENT_CASH -> add_cash_movement rolls back the legacy CashMovement too and returns 409, blocking all inkassa company-wide while the mode is on, or (b) if the stale balance suffices, writes two TRANSFER legs into a ledger that is otherwise not being written, desynchronizing it from the legacy movements recorded in the same period.
findings.evidence: retrofit.py:456 `if not cash_enabled(db) or float(amount or 0) <= 0: return None` (on_cash_collection) vs retrofit.py:472+ on_cash_op -> _shift_ctx -> `if not dual_write_enabled(db): return None, None`. mode.py documents LEGACY_ONLY as 'ledger'ga UMUMAN yozilmaydi'.

verdicts.reasoning: See above.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial only: apps/server/app/services/cash/tenant.py::require_ledger_writable (invoked via cutover_guard.require_custody_account on both collection paths) raises ERR_LEDGER_UNAVAILABLE in LEGACY_ONLY, but only for ledger-native tenants — it returns immediately for legacy/migration tenants. Also `from_till_id is None -> return None` in on_cash_collection no-ops pre-T0 unmapped shifts. Neither protects a legacy tenant with a till-bound shift, and posting.py::post_transfer contains no mode check.
verdicts.repro_hint: Pg test, legacy (non-native) tenant with provisioned TILL+SAFE: open shift (SHADOW), mode.set_mode("LEGACY_ONLY"), POST a cash sale (no IN leg written), then POST /shifts cash movement type=collection with destination_safe_id for an amount above the frozen ledger TILL balance -> expect 409 INSUFFICIENT_CASH and the legacy CashMovement rolled back; retry with a small amount -> expect 2 new TRANSFER rows in cash.cash_ledger_entries despite LEGACY_ONLY (contrast with test_mode_legacy_only_writes_no_ledger which shows count==0 for payin).

findings.title: retrofit.on_cash_op still maps kind='collection' to a single-leg OUT, contradicting the two-leg transfer contract in the same file
findings.claim: retrofit.py:434-439 (_CASHOP_MAP) documents that 'collection' must NOT be a one-legged manual_cash_out because it made safe-bound cash vanish from the company ledger total, yet the live dispatch dict inside on_cash_op (retrofit.py:470-471) still contains `"collection": adapters.manual_cash_out`.
findings.invariant: A collection never reduces total company custody; it must post as a TILL->SAFE transfer pair (single transfer_group), per §4/§14.
findings.attack_scenario: No current caller reaches it (shifts.py:117-131 and cashops.py:148-156 both special-case collection to on_cash_collection first), but any future or third call site that forwards a CashMovement kind straight to on_cash_op — the function signature explicitly advertises 'payin/payout/expense/collection' in its docstring — silently books OUT·CASH_OUT with no matching SAFE IN, understating company cash by the collection amount, immutably (append-only ledger).
findings.evidence: retrofit.py:470-471 `fn = {"payin": ..., "payout": ..., "expense": ..., "collection": adapters.manual_cash_out}.get(kind)` vs the corrected _CASHOP_MAP at :434-439 that deliberately omits collection with the comment 'Ilgari manual_cash_out edi: bir oyoqli OUT... LEDGER'DAN YO'QOLARDI'. _CASHOP_MAP itself is dead code.

verdicts.reasoning: The static facts in the finding are accurate: at SHA 482b3f38, apps/server/app/services/cash/retrofit.py on_cash_op's dispatch dict still contains "collection": adapters.manual_cash_out, its docstring advertises "collection", and _CASHOP_MAP (which deliberately omits collection with the explanatory comment) is dead code referenced only by comments/docs (phase0.py, phase1.py, MIGRATION_PHASE0.md). However, the financial-safety attack cannot be made concrete: git grep over apps/server at the SHA shows exactly two runtime callers of on_cash_op — apps/server/app/api/v1/cashops.py:157 and apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py:133 — and both sit in the else-arm of `if data.type == "collection"`, where the branch condition tests the very same variable later passed as kind. The collection arm in each caller routes to on_cash_collection (paired TILL->SAFE adapters.transfer, single transfer_group) after validating the destination SAFE (cutover_guard.require_custody_account in shifts.py; custody_preview.collection_source/collection_destination in cashops.py). So the protective constraint is call-site exhaustive special-casing: every path that can produce kind="collection" is intercepted before on_cash_op, and no third call site exists. The finding's own attack_scenario admits "No current caller reaches it" and rests entirely on a hypothetical future caller, which fails the concreteness bar. The dead dict entry and misleading docstring are real code-hygiene debt (a one-line cleanup would remove the latent footgun), but at this SHA no reachable path books a one-legged OUT for a collection, so company custody cannot be understated by this mechanism. (Separate, out-of-scope note: phase1.py _cashop_legs_and_review intentionally backfills historical collection movements as single-leg OUT·CASH_OUT — a documented pre-ledger design decision, not this finding.)
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Call-site exhaustive dispatch: the only two callers of on_cash_op (apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py:113-133 add_cash_movement, apps/server/app/api/v1/cashops.py:143-157) branch on `data.type == "collection"` — the identical value passed as `kind` — and route collection to retrofit.on_cash_collection (two-leg adapters.transfer with shared transfer_group, SAFE destination validated via require_custody_account / custody_preview helpers) before on_cash_op can be reached. No other caller of on_cash_op exists at the SHA.
verdicts.repro_hint: Verdict flips to CONFIRMED only if a new call site forwards a raw CashMovement kind to on_cash_op without the collection special-case; recommend deleting the "collection" key from the dict at retrofit.py:470-471 (or raising on it) and removing "collection" from the docstring as hardening.

findings.title: P9 offline-sale-policy skips the device-clock check unless force_shift is on, so a post-T0 store with a skewed clock still gets ALLOWED
findings.claim: The DEVICE_CLOCK_UNRELIABLE gate runs only `if required and client_time is not None` (shifts.py:414-425), where required = force_shift. For a post-T0 tenant with force_shift off, an open till-bound shift and a clock hours behind, the endpoint returns ALLOWED, but the replay's sold_at falls before shift.opened_at, so the historical shift lookup (services/sales.py:96-102) finds nothing and the cash sale is booked shift-less: OFF_SHIFT/TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW ledger anomaly and a Sale outside the shift (drawer surplus at close) — or a 400 TILL_REQUIRED dead-letter if the queued payload carries no usable till_id.
findings.invariant: The P9 commit's stated contract: the policy endpoint must say BLOCKED whenever the server is certain (or near-certain) to reject or misattribute the eventual replay of an offline sale.
findings.attack_scenario: Post-T0 store, force_shift off (owner never enabled it), POS CMOS clock 3 hours behind. Policy fetched -> ALLOWED (post-T0 branch passes because shift.till_id is set; clock branch skipped). Network drops; cashier takes cash offline all day. On reconnect every receipt replays with sold_at < opened_at, detaches from the shift, and lands as ledger exceptions / shift-less sales; the shift closes with a surplus equal to the day's offline cash.
findings.evidence: shifts.py:412-414 comment 'soat faqat MAJBURIY rejimda tekshiriladi' plus `if required and client_time is not None:`; the post-T0 block above (shifts.py:404-410) checks only shift/till existence, never the clock.

verdicts.reasoning:
The broken path is provable by reading code alone; no protective mechanism prevents it, only detect-and-repair mechanisms soften it.

Chain, verified at the SHA:
1. apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py::offline_sale_policy — the DEVICE_CLOCK_UNRELIABLE gate is literally `if required and client_time is not None:` with `required = _CPV.force_shift_on(db, emp.company_id)` (custody_preview.py:234 reads only the `security.force_shift` setting; post-T0/ledger-native does NOT imply it). The post-T0 block above checks only `shift is None` / `shift.till_id is None`, never the clock. With an open till-bound shift the endpoint returns ALLOWED regardless of a clock hours behind.
2. Client (packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts): ALLOWED is cached 8h (OFFLINE_POLICY_TTL_MS); the `if (now < p.at) return false` guard only catches a clock that jumps backward AFTER the stamp, not a constantly-behind CMOS clock. Queued sold_at = device time.
3. Replay: apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py::_clamp_sold_at keeps any past timestamp within 60 days, so the skewed sold_at survives. apps/server/app/services/sales.py::create_sale historical lookup (`Shift.opened_at <= now AND (closed_at IS NULL OR closed_at >= now)`, no tolerance) finds nothing when sold_at < opened_at → shift=None; force_shift off → no 400.
4. Post-T0 acceptance: the POS payload always carries till_id (packages/shared/src/screens/POSKassa.tsx:647 `till_id: currentTillId()`), and sales.py §4 uses the validated declared till when `shift is None` (`_till_id = _acc.id`), so `require_post_t0_till` passes and the Sale is written with shift_id=None. (The finding's alternate TILL_REQUIRED dead-letter branch is therefore unlikely for the stated till-bound-shift scenario.)
5. Ledger: services/cash/retrofit.py::on_cash_sale → posting.py::_resolve_shift with device_ts = sold_at; `_in_window` tolerance is only 60 min (CASH_TS_TOLERANCE_MIN), so a 3h-behind timestamp lands in Case B: posting_kind=OFF_SHIFT + TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception.
6. Surplus: services/cash/tenant.py::ledger_expected_shift_cash = opening_cash + repositories.py::shift_movement_total, which sums ON_SHIFT legs only — the OFF_SHIFT offline cash is physically in the drawer but excluded from expected → surplus at close.

Corrections to the finding's overstatements (they lower impact, not the verdict): (a) not "every receipt all day" — only receipts whose skewed sold_at precedes shift.opened_at detach from the Sale (and precedes opened_at−60min for the ledger leg); with a 3h skew that is roughly the first 3 hours of the shift. (b) It is not silent money loss: the replay is ACCEPTED (P9's "no lost transaction" goal holds), the anomaly is recorded as a TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception in the TILL OFF_SHIFT queue (cash_ddl_v1.sql:494-496) and can be attributed later via reconciliation_assignments — a repair channel, not a preventive constraint. The endpoint's own comment block enumerates exactly this hazard ("soat ORQADA va sold_at < shift.opened_at -> tarixiy izlash HECH NARSA topmaydi") yet the code enforces it only in force_shift mode, on the incorrect rationale that with the policy off "the sale gets written anyway" — true, but written as an OFF_SHIFT anomaly that corrupts the shift close. P2 stands.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Only mitigations, none preventive: (1) posting.py 60-min _TS_TOLERANCE_MIN window absorbs skew < ~1h for the ledger leg (but the business-shift lookup in sales.py has zero tolerance); (2) the OFF_SHIFT/TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception queue + reconciliation_assignments surface and allow manual repair of the misattribution; (3) sync.py _clamp_sold_at only rejects future>5min or >60-day-old timestamps — a behind clock passes.
verdicts.repro_hint: PG test: tenant with cash_enabled + cutover_reached, force_shift off; open a till-bound Shift at T; GET /shifts/offline-sale-policy?client_time=T-3h → expect {mode:"ALLOWED"} (the bug). Then POST /sync/push with a cash sale {sold_at: T-2h, till_id: <shift's till>} → sale accepted with Sale.shift_id NULL, cash_ledger_entries row posting_kind=OFF_SHIFT with TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception; ledger_expected_shift_cash for the open shift excludes the amount (surplus at close).

findings.title: Ledger append-only enforcement is trigger-only and the runtime credential can disable it (tenant_purge proves the capability)
findings.claim: The immutability triggers (cash_ddl_v1.sql:447-460) block row UPDATE/DELETE and TRUNCATE, and the DDL provisions a restricted `cash_posting` role (REVOKE UPDATE,DELETE at :529-536) — but the FastAPI runtime connects with a single DATABASE_URL role (db/session.py) that is the table owner: app/tools/tenant_purge.py:726 executes `ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER USER` on the cash tables with that same credential class. The triggers are plain (not ENABLE ALWAYS), so `SET session_replication_role = replica` or DISABLE TRIGGER from any code path running under the app credential bypasses append-only entirely.
findings.invariant: cash.cash_ledger_entries must be unmodifiable by the application credential; only INSERT via CashPostingService (and the audited backfill) should be possible.
findings.attack_scenario: Any SQL-injection foothold, compromised admin tool, or future maintenance script running under the app's DB user can silently rewrite or delete ledger legs (disable triggers, UPDATE amount, re-enable) — the append-only guarantee that shift reconciliation, T0 enforcement and backfill verification all assume is not enforced against the credential the app actually uses. Defense-in-depth (the cash_posting role) exists in DDL but is not what the runtime session runs as (phase0.py:666-668 checks the role's privileges, yet no SET ROLE happens at runtime).
findings.evidence: tenant_purge.py:693/726 (DISABLE TRIGGER USER executed via the app's Session); cash_ddl_v1.sql triggers declared without ENABLE ALWAYS; db/session.py builds one engine from DATABASE_URL with no role switching.

verdicts.reasoning: See above.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. Triggers are plain (not ENABLE ALWAYS); no event trigger guards ALTER TABLE; DDL role REVOKEs (cash_ddl_v1.sql §P) apply only to group roles the runtime never SET ROLEs into; phase0.py readiness checks role privileges but not the runtime connection's identity or ownership.
verdicts.repro_hint: On a Postgres instance initialized via `python -m app.initdb` with a single DATABASE_URL: open a session with the app's SessionLocal and run `ALTER TABLE cash.cash_ledger_entries DISABLE TRIGGER USER; UPDATE cash.cash_ledger_entries SET amount = amount + 1 WHERE id = <any>; ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE TRIGGER USER;` — it succeeds, exactly as tenant_purge.py's execute_purge already does. Fix direction: run migrations/initdb under a separate owner role and connect the runtime as a non-owner login granted only cash_posting/cash_app.

findings.title: UNIQUE(product_id, branch_id) on inventory is never ensured/verified at runtime, though the WH-017 create-and-lock race fix depends on it
findings.claim: The concurrent-first-sale protection in _create_sale_once (services/sales.py:270-280, 'QA WH-017') relies on the DB rejecting a second Inventory row for the same (product_id, branch_id): the loser is expected to hit IntegrityError at flush and re-run under the retry wrapper. That uniqueness exists only as a model-level UniqueConstraint (models/inventory.py:16), which materializes solely via create_all on a fresh table. Unlike ux_doc_counter, ux_alloc_item_lot, ux_sales_company_client_uuid etc., initdb.py never issues a CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS for inventory, and required_schema.py checks only the inventory.low_alerted column (:246) — so a production database whose inventory table predates or lost the constraint boots green.
findings.invariant: Exactly one Inventory row per (product_id, branch_id); the whole per-row FOR UPDATE stock-locking scheme assumes it (`.first()` locks 'the' row).
findings.attack_scenario: On a DB without the constraint: two POS terminals sell a just-created product simultaneously; both see no Inventory row, both INSERT one (no conflict), each locks and decrements its own row. Stock splits across two rows; every later query uses `.first()` nondeterministically, so decrements land on different rows — oversell passes the qty check and reported stock is permanently wrong.
findings.evidence: initdb.py:552-586 comments state the pattern explicitly ('Modelda UniqueConstraint bor, lekin uni FAQAT create_all chiqaradi; MAVJUD jadvalda cheklov paydo BO'LMAYDI') and add explicit unique indexes for other tables — but no such line exists for inventory (git grep 'inventory' initdb.py returns only the low_alerted column). required_schema.py:246 verifies no inventory index.
findings.suggested_repro: On PG, `\d inventory` in the production/staging clone to confirm the constraint exists; if absent, two concurrent sessions inserting Inventory rows for the same (product, branch) both succeed.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding's factual observations are accurate but its premise — "a production database whose inventory table predates or lost the constraint" — is counterfactual for this codebase; no such database can exist through any provisioning path the repo has ever shipped. Protective mechanism: the UNIQUE(product_id, branch_id) constraint is born WITH the inventory table on every creation path, in every version of the code. (1) apps/server/app/models/inventory.py has carried `__table_args__ = (UniqueConstraint("product_id", "branch_id"),)` since the project's very first commit 720c7e6 ("SavdoOS ... birinchi versiya", verified via `git grep UniqueConstraint 720c7e6 -- apps/server/app/models/*.py`), so every database ever materialized by `Base.metadata.create_all()` (the boot path, apps/server/app/initdb.py) created inventory with the constraint inline — create_all only skips EXISTING tables; it never creates one without its declared constraints. (2) The manual/reference DDL path db/schema.sql:270-281 likewise declares `UNIQUE (product_id, branch_id)` inside CREATE TABLE inventory. (3) No migration or repair tool ever rebuilds or alters the inventory table (`git grep -i inventory 482b3f3 -- apps/server/app/db/migrations apps/server/app/tools` returns nothing) and `git log -S inventory_product_id_branch_id --all` shows no code ever dropping it. This is exactly why initdb._ensure_indexes backfills ux_doc_counter, ux_alloc_item_lot, ux_smove_alloc etc. but not inventory: those tables existed BEFORE their uniqueness was added to the model (the initdb.py comments the finder quotes describe that retrofit situation), whereas inventory's uniqueness predates every deployed table. The WH-017 loser therefore does hit IntegrityError at flush on any real DB (services/sales.py, `db.add(Inventory(...)); db.flush()` after the sorted-lock loop), and the retry wrapper re-runs it as designed. The only way to reach the attack state is an operator manually dropping the constraint or a corrupted partial restore — speculation, not a concrete attack per the audit's default. Residual hygiene note (not a defect): adding the inventory key to core/required_schema.py REQUIRED/optional index verification (it currently checks only inventory.low_alerted at :246) would make even that operator-error scenario boot-red; cheap defense-in-depth, severity well below P2.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: UNIQUE(product_id, branch_id) is created together with the inventory table on both provisioning paths: models/inventory.py UniqueConstraint present since first commit 720c7e6 (materialized by create_all at table creation on every DB ever booted), and db/schema.sql:280 `UNIQUE (product_id, branch_id)` in CREATE TABLE inventory. No migration/tool in repo history rebuilds inventory or drops the constraint, so no upgrade path yields an inventory table without it.
verdicts.repro_hint: To close the residual hygiene gap, confirm on the production clone with `\d inventory` that inventory_product_id_branch_id_key exists (expected: yes), then consider listing it in apps/server/app/core/required_schema.py so a manually damaged schema fails readiness instead of booting green.

findings.title: Pre-T0 offline replay attaches a cash sale to an already-closed shift whose expected_cash is frozen — cash that no reconciliation ever demands
findings.claim: For offline replay (honor_price_snapshot=True, at=sold_at) the shift is found by `Shift.opened_at <= now AND (closed_at IS NULL OR closed_at >= now)` with NO status filter, so a sold_at inside a CLOSED shift attaches the sale there. The closed-shift rejection (`cutover_guard.reject_closed_shift_replay`, reached via require_post_t0_till) is a no-op whenever `enforcement_active` is False, i.e. for every tenant without cutover_at (all current legacy/production tenants). close_shift froze expected_cash at close time; shifts.py summary (QA SHIFT-4) deliberately shows the frozen value; the current open shift's expected only counts `Sale.shift_id == open_shift.id`. Result: the cash of the late sale is never included in ANY shift's expected cash.
findings.invariant: Every accepted cash sale must be demanded from exactly one drawer reconciliation (some shift's expected_cash must include it).
findings.attack_scenario: Pre-T0 tenant (cutover_at unset). Cashier makes a cash sale while offline (or simply crafts POST /sync/push with their kassa.sell token), keeps the receipt in the outbox until they close their shift (client-side Shift.tsx:246 outbox guard is same-device only and trivially bypassed by calling /shifts/{id}/close or /sync/push directly). counted==expected → clean close. Then the receipt flushes: sold_at falls inside the now-closed shift, sale+stock+revenue are written, but expected_cash of the closed shift is frozen and the open shift's expected excludes it. Cashier pockets the cash; books show revenue with zero shortage. sync.py::_clamp_sold_at allows sold_at up to 60 days back, so any past own-shift window works.
findings.evidence: sales.py:94-104 historic lookup without ShiftStatus filter; cutover_guard.py reject_closed_shift_replay: `if shift is None or not enforcement_active(db, company_id): return`; require_post_t0_till returns (None, False) before any check when `not enforcement_active`; and in sales.py the guard is only called `if _has_cash and _cr.cash_enabled(db)`. shifts.py close_shift freezes expected; shift_summary: `if s.status == closed and s.expected_cash is not None: expected = float(s.expected_cash)` — code comment on QA SHIFT-4/PAY-02 shows late-sync-into-closed-shift was known and only the DISPLAY was reconciled, not the cash custody. Memory note 'P9 offline smena xavfsizligi — yopilgan smena qoldiq xavfi, HOLD' confirms this is unresolved.

verdicts.reasoning: See above.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None effective for pre-T0 tenants. The only mechanism aimed at this exact attack, cutover_guard.reject_closed_shift_replay (ERR_CLOSED_SHIFT_REPLAY), is unreachable: require_post_t0_till returns (None, False) at `if not enforcement_active(db, company_id)` before calling it, and enforcement_active is False whenever cutover_at is unset; the guard is also skipped entirely when cash_enabled(db) is False. Secondary constraints checked and inert: require_ledger_writable no-ops for non-ledger-native tenants; close_shift's FOR UPDATE lock only serializes concurrent writes, not post-close replay; the dual-write ledger's LATE_SYNC/LATE_SYNC_UNACK exception (posting.py::_resolve_shift Case C) is a detection record only — shift_expected_cash counts ON_SHIFT legs only and the legacy frozen expected_cash is authoritative for the operator. Ledger-native tenants ARE protected (cutover_at set at creation), which matches the finding's pre-T0 scope.
verdicts.repro_hint: SQLite TestClient at the SHA (no Postgres needed, cash_enabled=False mirrors the weakest tenant): (1) open a shift as a cashier, make one cash sale of 100; (2) POST /shifts/{id}/close with counted_cash == expected (clean close, expected_cash frozen); (3) POST /sync/push with a new client_uuid, payment_method=cash, total 500, sold_at = a timestamp between opened_at and closed_at; assert the response is ok:true; (4) assert the new Sale.shift_id == the closed shift's id, GET /shifts/{id}/summary still returns the frozen expected (excluding the 500), and after opening+closing a new shift its expected also excludes the 500 — so no reconciliation anywhere demands the 500. Repeat with a Postgres+cash-schema tenant WITHOUT cutover_at to show require_post_t0_till returns before reject_closed_shift_replay; then set cutover_at and assert the same push now gets 400 CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY.

verdicts.reasoning:
Every link of the claimed chain is verifiable by reading the code at SHA 482b3f38, and I found no protective mechanism that breaks it for a tenant whose cutover_at is unset (or whose cash schema is absent).

1) Historic shift attach, no status filter — apps/server/app/services/sales.py, _create_sale_once. For honor_price_snapshot=True and at is not None (the exact combination /sync/push passes, apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py:58) the shift is selected by:
   `Shift.cashier_id == emp.id, Shift.opened_at <= now, (Shift.closed_at IS NULL | Shift.closed_at >= now)` (order_by opened_at desc). A sold_at inside the cashier's own already-CLOSED shift matches, and the sale is later written with `shift_id=shift.id if shift else None` — into the closed shift. The QA PAY-02 comment shows this is deliberate accounting-time attribution; custody was not addressed.

2) The closed-shift rejection is unreachable pre-T0 — apps/server/app/services/cash/cutover_guard.py. reject_closed_shift_replay opens with `if shift is None or not enforcement_active(db, company_id): return`, and enforcement_active returns False whenever `_cut.cutover_at(db, company_id)` is None (legacy tenants). Worse, require_post_t0_till returns `(None, False)` at `if not enforcement_active(...)` BEFORE it ever calls reject_closed_shift_replay, and in sales.py the guard call itself is gated by `if _has_cash and _cr.cash_enabled(db)` — for a tenant without the cash schema it is not even invoked. `_cg0.require_ledger_writable` (503 gate) is a no-op for non-ledger-native tenants (apps/server/app/services/cash/tenant.py: `if not is_ledger_native(...): return`).

3) expected_cash is frozen at close and never recomputed — apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py close_shift (line 568 `s.expected_cash = expected`) computes expected only from sales/movements committed at close time (under FOR UPDATE, so the late replay cannot race in — it arrives after commit). git grep shows the ONLY production writer of expected_cash is close_shift (plus demo_seed); there is no legacy-shift reopen endpoint and no recompute-on-late-attach hook.

4) The frozen value is authoritative for reporting — shifts.py shift_summary (line 231): `if s.status == ShiftStatus.closed and s.expected_cash is not None: expected = float(s.expected_cash)` (QA SHIFT-4 comment explicitly says late-synced offline sales are excluded so summary matches the frozen Z-report); shifts_overview line 321 likewise shows `float(s.expected_cash or 0)` with difference frozen at 0. The next open shift's live expected counts only `Sale.shift_id == open_shift.id` / `SalePayment` joined on that shift, so the late sale's cash appears in NO shift's expected. Revenue and stock, however, are fully committed (sales.py db.commit at line 737).

5) Dual-write does not rescue it — retrofit.on_cash_sale attaches the ledger leg via `_open_cash_shift_id` (the currently-open cash shift, or None), never posts LATE_SYNC and raises no exception; for legacy tenants dual_write_enabled is False and it is a no-op. LATE_SYNC exists only in DDL/design docs at this SHA (cash_ddl_v1.sql, EXECUTION_DESIGN.md), not in the runtime write path.

6) Feasibility — /sync/push needs only `require("kassa.sell")`; sold_at is client-supplied and _clamp_sold_at (sync.py:30) accepts anything in [now-60d, now+5m]; /shifts/{id}/close needs only get_current_employee with cashier_id==emp.id; the outbox hold-back guard is client-side only (no server-side pending-outbox check exists in shifts.py). So the cashier closes clean (counted==expected, sale not yet on server), then pushes the receipt: sale+revenue recorded, cash demanded from nobody.

The invariant "every accepted cash sale must be demanded by exactly one drawer reconciliation" is provably violated by static reading; the only trace is a passive inconsistency (closed shift's live naqd_sales/by_method exceed frozen expected-opening) that nothing flags. The memory note (P9 HOLD, late-sync recovery unbuilt at this SHA) is consistent with this being a known open hole.

findings.title: offline-sale-policy skips the device-clock check whenever force_shift is off — post-T0 stores get ALLOWED from a skewed device and the replay is then rejected or mis-custodied
findings.symbol: offline_sale_policy (line 413: `if required and client_time is not None`)
findings.claim: The DEVICE_CLOCK_UNRELIABLE evaluation (client_time > now+5min, or client_time < shift.opened_at) runs only when `required` (=force_shift) is on. The route's own post-T0 gate (lines 393-406) proves post-T0 tenants use this endpoint independently of force_shift, yet a post-T0/force_shift-off tenant with a clock-behind POS receives ALLOWED. The subsequent offline cash receipt carries sold_at < opened_at: if it lands inside the cashier's previous CLOSED shift, replay dies permanently with CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY (money already captured, dead-letter only); if it lands in a gap, the sale is accepted shift-less and its ledger leg posts OFF_SHIFT — excluded from every drawer's expected cash.
findings.invariant: P9 commit's stated contract: 'Refuse an offline sale the server is certain to reject' — the policy must return BLOCKED for any device state that makes the future replay deterministically fail or fall outside custody accounting.
findings.attack_scenario: Post-T0 store, force_shift off (independent settings). POS clock is 10 hours behind (CMOS/NTP fault). Policy returns ALLOWED (clock branch skipped since required=False). Cashier sells for cash offline; sold_at falls inside yesterday's closed shift of the same cashier. On flush, require_post_t0_till → reject_closed_shift_replay → 400 permanent → dead-letter. Money taken from the customer, no sale, no stock decrement, no cash leg — exactly the failure class the P9 commit was written to prevent.
findings.evidence: shifts.py:407-421: `if shift is None: return ALLOWED` (policy off) then `if required and client_time is not None:` guards both clock comparisons; the in-code rationale ('Siyosat o'chiq bo'lsa vaqt umuman ahamiyatsiz — smena topilmasa ham savdo yoziladi') predates/ignores the post-T0 §9 closed-shift rejection three paragraphs above in the same function. Server side: cutover_guard.reject_closed_shift_replay fires post-T0 for a closed shift found by the sold_at-historic lookup regardless of force_shift.
findings.suggested_repro: PG tenant with cutover_at set, force_shift off, cashier has a closed shift [d-1 09:00, d-1 18:00] and an open shift with till. GET /shifts/offline-sale-policy?client_time=<now-20h> → expect ALLOWED (bug). POST /sync/push with a cash sale, sold_at=d-1 12:00 → 400 CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY, retry=false.

verdicts.reasoning: Every step of the claimed path is verifiable by reading the SHA and is deterministic; no protective mechanism exists. (1) apps/server/app/api/v1/shifts.py::offline_sale_policy computes `required = _CPV.force_shift_on(...)` once; the post-T0 gate below it (`_cr.cash_enabled(db) and _cut.cutover_reached(...)`) runs independently of `required` — proving the route serves post-T0/force_shift-off tenants — but after that gate passes (open shift with valid till_id) the only clock evaluation is `if required and client_time is not None:`, so with force_shift off both DEVICE_CLOCK_UNRELIABLE comparisons (`ct > now+5min`, `ct < opened`) are skipped and the route returns ALLOWED for an arbitrarily skewed device clock. The in-code justification ("Siyosat o'chiq bo'lsa vaqt umuman ahamiyatsiz — smena topilmasa ham savdo yoziladi") is a pre-T0 rationale falsified by the post-T0 §9 rejection referenced three paragraphs above in the same function. (2) Client: packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts always sends client_time; offlineSaleAllowed's only clock defense is `if (now < p.at) return false`, which catches a clock stepped back AFTER caching but not a consistently-behind clock (p.at is stamped from the same skewed clock); the cached ALLOWED authorizes offline cash capture. (3) Replay: sync.py::_clamp_sold_at nulls only future>5min or >60-days-past values — an hours-behind sold_at passes through. services/sales.py::_create_sale_once (honor_price_snapshot) resolves the shift historically (`opened_at <= sold_at AND (closed_at IS NULL OR closed_at >= sold_at)`, cashier-scoped), excluding the current open shift. If sold_at lands in the cashier's prior CLOSED shift, require_post_t0_till → reject_closed_shift_replay (services/cash/cutover_guard.py:207) fires on enforcement_active alone (reads only cutover_at; force_shift is irrelevant) → _fail(ERR_CLOSED_SHIFT_REPLAY, status=400) → sync.py classifies 400 as permanent (retry=False) → dead-letter with money already captured, no sale/stock/ledger row (asserted by tests/test_offline_shift_policy_pg.py test 1). If sold_at lands in a gap, POSKassa.tsx sends `till_id: currentTillId()`, _create_sale_once adopts it for the shift-less case (`if _till_id is None and shift is None: _till_id = _acc.id`), the sale is accepted with shift_id=NULL, and cash_ddl_v1.sql's CHECK (line ~207: shift_id IS NULL ⇒ posting_kind='OFF_SHIFT') puts the cash leg outside every shift's expected-cash, into the OFF_SHIFT anomaly queue — mis-custodied exactly as claimed (surfaced, not silent, but still a custody deviation the policy promised to pre-block). Protective mechanisms hunted and absent: the DEVICE_CLOCK_UNRELIABLE check exists but is gated on the wrong condition; no other code path evaluates client_time; no clamp for behind-clocks; reject_closed_shift_replay is deliberately permanent (no auto-reattachment, no LATE_SYNC recovery yet); test_offline_shift_policy_pg.py covers post-T0 shift-less/till-less BLOCKs and the shift-closed-later race but has no clock-skew-with-force_shift-off case. The route's own post-T0 gate demonstrates the stated contract ("refuse what replay will deterministically reject") applies to force_shift-off tenants, and the closed-shift-landing failure is exactly as deterministic as the TILL_REQUIRED cases it does block — the guard condition should be `client_time is not None and (required or post-T0-cash-enforced)`. Severity note: the closed-shift arm needs the skew to overlap a prior closed shift of the same cashier (large skews or overnight shifts); the gap arm occurs for any behind-skew that exits the open shift's window.

findings.title: Client-supplied device_occurred_at steers the ledger posting_kind: out-of-window cash sale legs post OFF_SHIFT and vanish from ledger-native expected cash
findings.claim: posting._in_window classifies a TILL leg ON_SHIFT only when device_ts (client sold_at, clamped merely to [-60d, +5min] by sync.py::_clamp_sold_at) is within [shift.opened_at - 60min, opened_at + 24h + 60min]. Case B (open shift, out of window) posts OFF_SHIFT with only a TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception row. shift_movement_total — the sole input to ledger_expected_shift_cash (tenant.py:179), which OVERRIDES the legacy formula in close_shift for ledger-native tenants — sums ON_SHIFT legs only. So (a) any shift kept open longer than ~25h silently stops accruing expected cash for genuine online sales (device_ts=server now), and (b) an offline replay with backdated sold_at lands its real cash leg OFF_SHIFT while the sale is accepted.
findings.invariant: On a ledger-native tenant, every accepted cash-sale leg on a till must raise some shift's expected cash; posting classification of real money must not be steerable by an unauthenticated client timestamp.
findings.attack_scenario: Ledger-native post-T0 store, force_shift off. Variant A (no clock tricks): cashier leaves the shift open 26h (24/7 kiosk or deliberate); every cash sale after hour 25 posts OFF_SHIFT; at close, expected = opening + ON_SHIFT movements only → cashier pockets all later cash sales, Z-report closes clean; only unreviewed cash_exceptions rows record the anomaly. Variant B: POST /sync/push with sold_at backdated into an off-hours gap (no shift matches historically) plus the valid till_id → sale accepted shift-less, leg OFF_SHIFT, same clean-close theft.
findings.evidence: posting.py:53-54 (`CASH_MAX_SHIFT_HOURS=24`, `CASH_TS_TOLERANCE_MIN=60`), :336 `return OFF_SHIFT, None, ["TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW"]  # Case B`; repositories.py:100 filters `posting_kind == ON_SHIFT`; tenant.py ledger_expected_shift_cash returns opening + shift_movement_total and shifts.py close_shift takes it as authoritative (`if _led is not None: expected = _led`). Nothing closes or blocks a >24h shift; nothing gates OUT-of-window IN legs at acceptance time.

verdicts.reasoning: See above.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None preventing the defect. Existing mechanisms are detective only: CashLedgerException rows (TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW / UNRESOLVED_OFF_SHIFT), the partial index cle_ix_off_shift "anomaly queue", and manager+ lifecycle.assign_off_shift (logical attribution that never changes entry.shift_id or shift_movement_total). No shift-duration cap, no auto-close, no close-time gate on open exceptions, no acceptance-time rejection of out-of-window IN legs, no DDL trigger requiring SALE legs to be ON_SHIFT.
verdicts.repro_hint: PG only (cash schema is Postgres-only). Ledger-native tenant, dual-write on, T0 reached, force_shift off. Variant A: open cash+legacy shift on a till; UPDATE cash.shifts SET opened_at = now()-interval '26 hours' (or monkeypatch posting._now); POST a normal online cash sale; assert cash_ledger_entries row for the sale has posting_kind='OFF_SHIFT', shift_id NULL, plus a TIMESTAMP_OUT_OF_WINDOW exception; close the shift with counted = opening → expected_cash excludes the sale, difference = 0. findings.title: Post-T0: honest offline receipts are permanently unrecoverable if the shift is closed before the outbox flushes (cross-device close or direct API), and the server has no pending-sync close guard
findings.claim: The offline-sale-policy's own justification ('an open-now shift later closed still accepts the replay because the historic lookup allows closed_at >= sold_at') is broken post-T0: reject_closed_shift_replay rejects EVERY cash replay into a closed shift with a permanent 400, even when sold_at is genuinely inside the shift window. The only protection is client-side (Shift.tsx:246 blocks close while outboxAll() is non-empty) and exists only on the device holding the outbox. close_shift on the server accepts unconditionally, and the promised LATE_SYNC recovery flow is explicitly not built (T0_CUTOVER_ENFORCEMENT.md line ~177: 'no code path creates LATE_SYNC entries today').
findings.invariant: A cash sale legitimately completed under an ALLOWED policy while the shift was open must eventually be recordable on the server (no permanently lost, money-captured transactions).
findings.attack_scenario: Post-T0 store. Cashier sells offline on terminal A (policy ALLOWED, shift open). Power dies on A; cashier closes the shift from terminal B (empty outbox there — close guard passes) or the manager closes via direct POST /shifts/{id}/close from the cashier's session. Terminal A comes back, flushes: sold_at is inside the now-closed shift → CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY, retry=false → dead-letter. Money was taken; no server-side sale, stock decrement, or cash leg exists, and no recovery mechanism can ever admit it — only the two-step-clearable localStorage dead-letter list holds the evidence.
findings.evidence: shifts.py close_shift performs no outbox/pending check (it cannot — the queue is client-side) and no delayed-close grace; cutover_guard.reject_closed_shift_replay fails on `status == closed or closed_at is not None` with status 400 (sync.py marks 400 permanent, dead-letter); offline_sale_policy's comment block (shifts.py ~355-365) still claims the closed-shift replay path is safe. T0 doc: 'Future LATE_SYNC recovery boundary … deliberately not built here.'

verdicts.reasoning: Every link of the claimed path is verifiable by reading the SHA. (1) Post-T0 gate: cutover_guard.reject_closed_shift_replay (apps/server/app/services/cash/cutover_guard.py:207-224) rejects when `st == ShiftStatus.closed.value or getattr(shift, "closed_at", None) is not None` — it never consults sold_at, so an in-window honest replay is rejected identically to a tampered one; _fail raises HTTP 400 (default status=400) with code CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY. (2) The replay reaches it: services/sales.py create_sale, for offline replay (honor_price_snapshot and at is not None), resolves the shift HISTORICALLY (`opened_at <= now AND (closed_at IS NULL OR closed_at >= now)`) — deliberately finding the closed shift — and for cash calls cutover_guard.require_post_t0_till(shift=shift), whose first step is reject_closed_shift_replay, raised BEFORE the Sale row or any ledger leg is written. (3) Permanence: sync.py::push marks `_transient = e.status_code >= 500 or e.status_code == 409`; the 400 returns retry:false and packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts:189-191 dead-letters and removes it from the outbox. (4) No server close guard: shifts.py::close_shift (line ~531) checks only cashier ownership + status==open under FOR UPDATE; there is no pending-sync/grace condition (and cannot be — the outbox is client-side). The only guard is Shift.tsx:246 `if (outboxAll().length > 0)`, per-device localStorage; its own comment calls it "faqat ... UX qatlami". The same cashier logged into terminal B has an empty local outbox and closes the shift freely, making the attack concrete without any malice. (5) No recovery mechanism exists: posting.py::_resolve_shift Case C does emit LATE_SYNC for a closed in-window CashShift, but it is unreachable for a sale replay because require_post_t0_till raises first; lifecycle.py::reopen_shift is not exposed by any API route (no hits in apps/server/app/api) and operates on cash.CashShift, not the legacy Shift row the guard inspects; no code sets Shift.status back to open. Both design docs confirm: T0_CUTOVER_ENFORCEMENT.md ("deliberately no automatic path" to LATE_SYNC) and FRESH_PRODUCTION_LAUNCH.md §5a ("A full LATE_SYNC approval workflow remains post-launch work"). (6) The offline_sale_policy justification comment (shifts.py:349-355: an open-now shift later closed still accepts the replay via the historical lookup) is factually stale post-T0 — the policy returns ALLOWED for an open shift with a till and does not model close-before-flush. One correction to the finding: a manager CANNOT close another cashier's shift via POST /shifts/{id}/close (`s.cashier_id != emp.id` -> 404); only the cross-device same-cashier close variant works, which is sufficient. Severity context: the loss is not silent (durable dead-letter savdoos_outbox_failed + red badge, and the drawer shows a counted-cash surplus at close) and is a documented, accepted launch residual — but the invariant as stated (an ALLOWED-policy cash sale must eventually be recordable server-side) is violated: no server-side sale, stock decrement, or cash leg can ever be created for that receipt through any existing code path.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial mitigations only, none preventing the loss: (a) client-side close guard Shift.tsx:246 — per-device localStorage, bypassed by closing from any other device/session of the same cashier; (b) permanent-vs-transient split in sync.py + sync.ts deadLetter preserves the receipt payload durably client-side (evidence, not recovery); (c) the un-synced cash appears as a counted>expected surplus in the Z-report at close (detection, not recovery); (d) posting.py LATE_SYNC Case C and lifecycle.reopen_shift exist but are unreachable for this flow (guard raises pre-posting; reopen has no API route and targets cash.CashShift, not the legacy Shift the guard checks).

Device A flush: POST /sync/push with the sale -> result {ok:false, retry:false, code:"CLOSED_SHIFT_CASH_REPLAY_REQUIRES_RECOVERY"}; assert no Sale row, no stock decrement, no cash_ledger_entries leg, and no endpoint that can subsequently admit the receipt.
