findings.title: Guard cache keyed on id(bind) with no eviction: entries survive engine disposal, id() reuse can leak a verdict across databases, and the dict grows unboundedly
findings.claim: The module-global cache key is (id(bind), index, table) and entries are never evicted (only overwritten or reset_cache()). id() of a garbage-collected Engine/Connection can be reassigned to a new bind pointing at a different database within the TTL, in which case a cached OK for database A is served for database B (or a cached BAD wrongly refuses B's writes). Additionally every distinct bind adds permanent entries, so processes that create many engines/connections (multi-tenant probes, pgserver-per-test suites — session.get_bind() returns the Connection when a session is connection-bound, and connection objects recycle fast) both grow the dict without bound and maximize id-reuse odds. test_BIND_boyicha_ALOHIDA_keshlanadi only proves two simultaneously-live objects get distinct keys.
findings.invariant: A schema-guarantee verdict must be attributable to the database it was verified against for the entire time it is served from cache.
findings.attack_scenario: A worker verifies ux_doc_counter OK against DB-A via a short-lived Engine/Connection, the object is GC'd, and within 10s a new Connection to DB-B (whose ux_doc_counter is non-unique after a botched rebuild) is allocated at the same address; require_index serves the stale OK and the write proceeds unguarded on DB-B. In production the single module-global engine makes this unreachable on the main path, so impact is confined to connection-bound sessions and multi-engine tooling — hardening, not an active exploit.
findings.evidence: index_guard.py: `_cache: dict[tuple[int, str, str], ...]`, `key = (id(bind), index, table)`; no weakref, no eviction; _bind_of returns db.get_bind(), which is a Connection for connection-bound sessions.

verdicts.reasoning: The cache-key mechanics are as described (apps/server/app/core/index_guard.py: `_cache: dict[tuple[int, str, str], ...]`, `key = (id(bind), index, table)`, no eviction), but the attack requires a bind object to be garbage-collected and its id() reassigned to a bind of a DIFFERENT database within the 10s TTL, while both are probed for the same (index, table). No code path at SHA 85be3991 can produce that. Protective facts: (1) Every require_index call site — apps/server/app/services/doc_seq.py:146, app/services/subscription/lifecycle.py:331, app/services/subscription/payments.py:71 — receives the request Session from `get_db()`/`SessionLocal`, and apps/server/app/db/session.py defines `SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, ...)` over a single MODULE-GLOBAL `engine = create_engine(_url, **_engine_kw)`. `Session.get_bind()` on an engine-bound session returns that Engine, which is permanently referenced by the module and can never be GC'd, so id() reuse is impossible and the cache is bounded at exactly one bind-id x 3 guarded indexes — no unbounded growth in any deployed process. (2) The finding's connection-bound-session premise ("get_bind() returns the Connection") is not exercised anywhere: git grep at the SHA shows every sessionmaker in app and tests is engine-bound (`sessionmaker(bind=eng/engine/pg/legacy_db)`); no `bind=conn`/connection-bound session exists. (3) The only multi-engine code paths are the offline 1C migrator (app/tools/migrate_1c.py, one target engine held for the whole run) and pg test fixtures (engines held by fixture references for their lifetime), so old and new binds are simultaneously live with distinct ids; test files additionally call `ig.reset_cache()` (tests/test_index_guarantee_guard.py, tests/test_subscription_migration_pg.py). (4) Even in the hypothetical collision, exposure is capped by the 10s TTL, and the underlying real unique index — not the guard — remains the actual duplicate barrier; the guard only converts a missing-index TOCTOU into a clean 409. The finder itself concedes "In production the single module-global engine makes this unreachable on the main path... hardening, not an active exploit" at low confidence. Per the default rule, an attack that cannot be made concrete is REFUTED; a weakref-keyed or TTL-pruned cache would be a reasonable hardening cleanup, not a financial-integrity defect.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Single module-global Engine (apps/server/app/db/session.py: `engine = create_engine(...)`, `SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, ...)`) is the only bind ever passed to index_state by any require_index call site; being module-referenced it is never GC'd, so id() reuse and cross-database key collision are unreachable, and the cache is bounded at one bind-id per process. Secondary: no connection-bound sessions exist at the SHA, 10s TTL caps any stale verdict, and `reset_cache()` is invoked by the multi-engine test suites.
verdicts.repro_hint: To even simulate the claim one must artificially create engine A to DB-A, prime the cache via index_state, drop every reference and force gc, then loop-allocate engines to DB-B until id() collides with A's — a manufactured condition with no corresponding code path in app or tooling at this SHA.

findings.title: SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL is unvalidated: an arbitrarily large value silently extends the unguarded stale-positive window, and a malformed value turns every guarded money write into an import-time 500
findings.claim: `_TTL_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL", "10") or 10)` is evaluated at module import with no upper bound, no lower bound, and no error handling. Setting it to e.g. 86400 makes the documented 10s stale-positive window (during which a dropped/broken index goes undetected and writes proceed unguarded) a full day per process, defeating the guard's core tradeoff without any warning at boot or in readiness. A non-numeric value ('10s', '') raises ValueError at import, and since the three call sites import lazily inside the function (doc_seq.py:143), the first sale/enrol/payment after deploy fails with an unhandled 500 (not the designed 409) on every request until the env var is fixed.
findings.invariant: The stale-positive window is the guard's security parameter; misconfiguration must not be able to silently widen it beyond an intended bound, and configuration errors must fail at boot, not per-write.
findings.attack_scenario: An operator 'tuning away' guard overhead sets SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL=3600 on Railway. Later a REINDEX mishap invalidates ux_doc_counter; readiness turns red but each worker keeps serving its hour-old OK verdict, so sales keep allocating receipt numbers with no unique barrier — the exact scenario the guard was built to refuse — for up to an hour per worker.
findings.evidence: index_guard.py:63 (module-level float(...) of raw env, no clamp, no try/except); positive and negative verdicts share the same TTL by design, so the widened window applies to OK verdicts.

verdicts.reasoning: No protective mechanism exists; both arms of the claim are provable by reading the code at the SHA. (1) TTL widening: apps/server/app/core/index_guard.py:62 reads `_TTL_SECONDS = float(os.getenv("SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL", "10") or 10)` with no upper bound, no clamp, no warning. `git grep` at the SHA shows the env var is referenced nowhere else in apps/server/app — no boot validation, no settings-layer check, no readiness exposure of the effective TTL. The positive (OK) verdict is cached under this same TTL (`_cache[key] = (now, OK)`, hit check `(now - hit[0]) < _TTL_SECONDS` in `index_state`), so TTL=86400 or even 'inf' (float() accepts it) makes a cached OK verdict survive an index drop for that whole window per process. `reset_cache()` is called only from tests (test_index_guarantee_guard.py, test_subscription_migration_pg.py) — there is no production-side cache invalidation other than TTL expiry. (2) Import-time crash: `float('10s')` raises ValueError during module execution. All three production call sites import lazily inside the hot function — apps/server/app/services/doc_seq.py:143 (`allocate`, guarding ux_doc_counter before every receipt-number allocation), apps/server/app/services/subscription/lifecycle.py:330, apps/server/app/services/subscription/payments.py:70 — and nothing imports index_guard at boot (main.py and required_schema.py only mention it in comments). Python evicts a module whose top-level execution failed from sys.modules, so every guarded write re-attempts the import, re-raises ValueError, and surfaces as an unhandled 500 instead of the designed 409, on every request until the env var is fixed; boot and /health/ready never notice. Two precision corrections to the finding: (a) the empty-string case does NOT crash — `os.getenv(..., "10") or 10` maps '' to 10; (b) the malformed-value arm fails CLOSED (writes are refused, so it is an availability defect, not a money-integrity one), and a negative or NaN TTL also fails safe (cache never valid, every write re-checks the catalog). The financially dangerous arm is only the unbounded-large-TTL one, which requires an operator with Railway env access and exercises a knob the docstring itself advertises as configurable ('oyna QISQA va SOZLANADI') — so severity P2 (hardening: clamp + parse-at-boot), not a remotely triggerable integrity break.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. Searched at the SHA for: boot/settings validation of SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL (absent — the var is read only at index_guard.py:62); an eager import of index_guard at app startup that would convert the ValueError into a boot failure (absent — all imports are function-local); production callers of reset_cache() that would invalidate a stale OK verdict (absent — tests only); readiness integration that blocks writes (explicitly disclaimed in the module docstring: /health/ready is monitoring-only). The unique index ux_doc_counter itself is the underlying barrier, but the guard exists precisely for the state where that index is missing/broken, so it does not mitigate the widened stale-OK window.
verdicts.repro_hint: Static proof suffices. If a runtime demo is wanted later: set SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL=10s, start the app (boots clean), then POST any sale — doc_seq.allocate's `from app.core.index_guard import require_index` raises ValueError('could not convert string to float') → 500, repeating on every request. For the TTL arm: set TTL=86400, make one sale (caches OK), drop ux_doc_counter, observe subsequent sales still allocate numbers while /health/ready is red.

findings.title: Live money-write idempotency indexes are neither boot-fatal nor write-guarded: total absence survives boot and duplicate offline replays write money twice
findings.claim: The fail-closed principle index_guard was built for ('readiness red blocks no writes, so the write itself must refuse') is applied only to doc_seq and two subscription services that have no HTTP route at this SHA, while the actually-live money paths (/sales, /sync/push, /returns, /cash/ops, customer/supplier payments, stock transfers) depend on IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES (required_schema.py:546-560), a class that is NOT in REQUIRED_INDEXES, is never boot-fatal even when the index is completely absent (initdb._verify_required_schema ~:2080 prints 'TAYYOR EMAS (boot davom etadi)' and continues), and has no require_index call anywhere under app/api (grep for require_index at 85be3991 returns only doc_seq.py:146, lifecycle.py:331, payments.py:71).
findings.invariant: A financial write whose only DB-level duplicate barrier is a unique index must be refused (fail-closed) when that barrier is provably absent — the stated owner rule of index_guard.py ('kafolatga tayangan yozuv SHU YERDA rad etiladi').
findings.attack_scenario: Legacy production DB where ux_sales_company_client_uuid (or ux_cashmov_client_uuid_all — required_schema.py:1404-1412 explicitly anticipates it failing to build over pre-existing duplicate keys) is missing. Boot succeeds, only /health/ready is red. Two POS devices (or one device double-flushing its outbox) POST /sync/push the same offline sale (same client_uuid) concurrently. _create_sale_once (services/sales.py:59-63) does SELECT-dedup then INSERT with no row lock keyed on client_uuid; under READ COMMITTED both misses. With the index absent no IntegrityError fires, both commit: two Sale rows, inventory decremented twice, on_cash_sale posts the cash ledger leg twice, two receipt numbers consumed. Writes stay unblocked indefinitely until an operator manually fixes the index.
findings.evidence: index_guard.py docstring: '/health/ready — monitoring signali, u hech qanday yozuvni to'smaydi'. required_schema.py:556-560 (authors' own words): 'Bu indeks yo'q bo'lsa /cash/ops dedupи faqat SELECT'ga tayanadi — parallel ikki takror ikki pul yozishi mumkin'. IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES excluded from _fatal (required_schema.py:843-851 iterates REQUIRED_INDEXES only). sales.py:46-50 retry wrapper catches only IntegrityError — with the index gone there is nothing to catch.
findings.suggested_repro: On PG: create schema, DROP INDEX ux_sales_company_client_uuid; boot app (no fatal); from two sessions concurrently POST /sync/push with identical client_uuid sale; assert two sales rows and doubled stock movement.

verdicts.reasoning: dup
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial mechanisms only, none sufficient: (a) initdb.py:722 re-attempts CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ux_sales_company_client_uuid every boot — heals fresh/clean DBs but silently skips on failure (duplicate keys / invalid index), the exact attack precondition; (b) /health/ready idempotency_schema key goes red — monitoring only, blocks nothing (index_guard.py docstring says so itself); (c) lot_policy.activation_readiness blocks /lots/enable when idempotency indexes are missing — gates lot activation, not sales/sync writes; (d) doc_seq's require_index on ux_doc_counter runs on every sale but guards a different index; (e) inventory with_for_update locks serialize concurrent sales but the client_uuid dedup SELECT precedes them and is never re-executed, so serialization does not restore idempotency.
verdicts.repro_hint: On PG with app schema: insert two rows into sales with equal (company_id, client_uuid) is impossible while index exists — first DROP INDEX ux_sales_company_client_uuid; restart app (observe boot succeeds, log shows "TAYYOR EMAS (boot davom etadi)"; note boot will try to recreate the index, so either pre-seed duplicate (company_id, client_uuid) sale rows so the CREATE fails 23505, or drop it after boot); then from two DB sessions/threads concurrently POST /sync/push with an identical sale payload (same client_uuid) and pause one transaction between the dedup SELECT and commit (e.g. via a lock on the inventory row) to hold the race window open; assert 2 sales rows, doubled sale_out stock_movements, doubled cash ledger legs.

verdicts.reasoning:
Every factual claim in the finding checks out at 85be3991, and every candidate protective mechanism is demonstrably absent by reading the actual execution path.

1) Not boot-fatal. `IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES` (apps/server/app/core/required_schema.py:546-563, includes `ux_sales_company_client_uuid`) is consumed only by `idempotency_missing()` (required_schema.py:1418-1440), whose docstring says "Boot'ni YIQITMAYDI va missing() ga KIRMAYDI". `initdb._verify_required_schema` prints these as "[schema] TAYYOR EMAS (boot davom etadi)" and continues; `_fatal()` (required_schema.py:843-870) iterates `REQUIRED_INDEXES` only.

2) Absence survives boot. `initdb._index` (initdb.py:351-381) does `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ux_sales_company_client_uuid` each boot, but on failure for a non-REQUIRED index it prints "[migrate] {name} — o'tkazib yuborildi ({e})" and continues. So on a legacy DB where sales already contains duplicate (company_id, client_uuid) pairs (written before the index existed, or during any absent window — the same class the authors document for ux_cashmov_client_uuid_all at required_schema.py:1404-1412), the CREATE fails with 23505 every boot and the index stays absent indefinitely; likewise on DDL-lock exhaustion (5 attempts, then skip). Only /health/ready goes red.

3) No write-side guard. `git grep require_index` at this SHA: only services/doc_seq.py:146 (guards ux_doc_counter), services/subscription/lifecycle.py:331 and payments.py:71 (no HTTP route wired). Nothing under app/api or in services/sales.py guards ux_sales_company_client_uuid, despite index_guard.py's own docstring stating "/health/ready — monitoring signali, u hech qanday yozuvni to'smaydi" and "yozuv SHU YERDA rad etiladi".

4) The runtime interleaving is real and unprotected. `push` (api/v1/sync.py:44) is a sync def endpoint (threadpool → true concurrency across requests/workers) calling `create_sale` per item. `_create_sale_once` (services/sales.py) runs the client_uuid dedup SELECT at the very top with no lock keyed on client_uuid and never re-checks it. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent replays of the same client_uuid both miss. The mechanisms that later serialize the two transactions do NOT rescue the dedup: (a) receipt_no is `_DS.tmp_value(_DS.SALE)` = "TMP-...-uuid4" — the inline comment explicitly says the old plain "TMP" value used to make parallel same-company sales collide on UNIQUE(company_id, receipt_no) and that this serialization was deliberately removed; (b) `_DS.allocate` takes a row lock on doc_counters via UPDATE...RETURNING and hands the second transaction a fresh, distinct number after the first commits — no IntegrityError; (c) Inventory `with_for_update` serializes the stock writes but both decrements apply. The `create_sale` retry wrapper (sales.py:41-50) catches only IntegrityError — with the index absent nothing raises it. Both transactions commit: two Sale rows with the same client_uuid, inventory decremented twice, two StockMovement rows, two receipt numbers, and `on_cash_sale` (called per sale after the explicit flush, sales.py ~685) posts the cash ledger leg twice. No advisory lock exists anywhere in the sale path (grep: advisory locks only in cash deploy and receipt/jobs reprint numbering).

With the index present, the second INSERT would block on the first's index tuple and get 23505 at commit, and the retry's re-run of the dedup SELECT would return the existing sale — proving the unique index is the sole duplicate barrier, exactly as initdb.py:721 comments ("race'ga chidamli DB-darajali dedup").

One refinement to the finding's repro: a bare DROP INDEX is healed at the next boot by the IF NOT EXISTS create, so the persistent-absence state requires either no restart, or pre-existing duplicate keys / a busy DDL lock making the create fail-and-skip. This narrows the precondition but does not refute it — the authors' own comments acknowledge that exact state as reachable, and while the app runs nothing re-checks the index.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None on this path. The only fail-closed write guards at this SHA are require_index on ux_doc_counter (doc_seq), ux_subscriptions_company, and ux_subpay_client_uuid — none covers the sales/returns/cash/payments idempotency indexes. Boot-time CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS in initdb heals a clean drop across restarts, but silently skips on duplicate-key failure or DDL-lock exhaustion, which is precisely the legacy state the finding targets.
verdicts.repro_hint: On PG: seed sales with two rows sharing (company_id, client_uuid) then DROP INDEX ux_sales_company_client_uuid (or just don't restart after the drop); boot — observe "[migrate] ux_sales_company_client_uuid — o'tkazib yuborildi" / "TAYYOR EMAS (boot davom etadi)", no fatal. From two threads POST /sync/push with an identical new client_uuid sale, pausing thread 1 after its dedup SELECT (e.g. breakpoint or lock on the inventory row) until thread 2 has passed its own dedup. Assert: 2 rows in sales for that client_uuid, inventory decremented 2x, 2 stock_movements, 2 cash ledger legs.

findings.title: Present-but-degraded REQUIRED indexes (invalid/non-unique/wrong shape) block nothing on the lot/receiving money writers — index_guard covers only 3 of ~17 registered financial indexes
findings.symbol: require_index call-site coverage (ux_lot_intake_key, ux_recv_corr_client, ux_lsr_request_client, ux_smove_alloc, ux_ret_alloc_line)
findings.claim: Per the 2026-09-29 owner decision, a REQUIRED index that exists by name but is not unique / invalid (failed CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY leaves exactly this state) or has the wrong columns/predicate only turns readiness red — boot proceeds (required_schema.py:843-870, _fatal checks presence only, soft class for the rest). The write-side compensation, index_guard.require_index, is wired at exactly three sites (doc_seq, subscription enrol, subscription payment). Every other REQUIRED/financial index writer — lot intake (ux_lot_intake_key, 'yagona DB to'siq' per required_schema.py:432-436), receiving corrections (ux_recv_corr_client, services/lot_correction.py: double reversal moves stock, debt AND cash twice per its own comment), shortfall resolutions, sale/return/movement lot allocations — performs SELECT-then-INSERT with no guard, so during index degradation their documented double-write failure modes are live.
findings.invariant: If a soft-classed (non-boot-fatal) index state can coexist with accepted writes, every writer whose correctness depends on that index must re-verify it fail-closed — otherwise the soft-boot decision silently converts a schema problem into double stock/money.
findings.attack_scenario: Operator runs REINDEX/CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on stock_batches during business hours and it fails, leaving ux_lot_intake_key INVALID (indisvalid=false: enforces nothing). Boot stays green, readiness red, nobody blocks POST /receiving/commit. A flaky network makes the Manager client retry the same receiving commit; two requests race the SELECT dedup window in create_lots; with the index invalid both INSERT succeed: the same delivery creates two stock batches, inventory doubled, supplier debt doubled. Same pattern for /receiving/{id}/corrections (double money reversal).
findings.evidence: required_schema.py:843-849: 'indeks NOMI YO'Q -> HALOKATLI; nomi bor, lekin NOYOB EMAS / YAROQSIZ -> TAYYORLIK QIZIL... QAMROV: yozuv tomonini index_guard.require_index fail-closed qiladi, LEKIN u FAQAT SIMLANGAN yo'llarda ishlaydi.' git grep require_index at 85be3991 confirms only doc_seq.py:146, lifecycle.py:331, payments.py:71 — none of the lot/receiving writers. IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES comment (:526) documents the exact failure: 'hisobdan chiqarish qoldiqni 2x kamaytiradi'.
findings.suggested_repro: On PG: UPDATE pg_index SET indisvalid=false WHERE indexrelid='ux_lot_intake_key'::regclass (simulating failed CONCURRENTLY); boot; two concurrent identical /receiving/commit payloads; assert two stock_batches for one client_uuid.

verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Layered, index-independent guards on every named writer: (1) receiving.py `_commit_once` — Supplier row `with_for_update()` taken before any stock/money write serializes identical retries, so `create_lots`'s dedup SELECT re-reads after the winner's commit; (2) `ux_receivings_client_uuid` on `receivings` (IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES, a different table than the degraded stock_batches index) aborts the losing transaction wholesale at db.commit(), with an explicit IntegrityError→rollback→duplicate:true handler; (3) `stock_invariant` gate inside the open transaction (409+rollback on inventory-vs-batch mismatch); (4) lot_correction.py:789/798/815 and lot_resolution.py:326-339 — document-row FOR UPDATE followed by a `_replay` dedup re-check under the exclusive lock. Additionally, PG itself: an invalid-but-ready index (the state the repro creates) still enforces uniqueness on inserts.
verdicts.repro_hint: To make any residual version of this concrete you would need a compound failure: make BOTH ux_lot_intake_key (stock_batches) and ux_receivings_client_uuid (receivings) non-enforcing (indisready=false, not just indisvalid=false), then race two /receiving/commit payloads that share client_uuid but name DIFFERENT supplier_ids (defeating the supplier-lock serialization) with only untracked products (defeating the stock invariant) — at which point it is a different, multi-index finding, not the one under test.

verdicts.reasoning: The coverage fact is true (git grep at 85be3991 confirms require_index is wired only in doc_seq.py:146, subscription/lifecycle.py:331, subscription/payments.py:71), but the claim that the named lot/receiving writers are therefore unprotected during index degradation does not survive the actual execution paths. (1) Attack scenario (invalid ux_lot_intake_key -> double /receiving/commit): in apps/server/app/api/v1/receiving.py _commit_once, purchase + stock_batches + Receiving header are one transaction; db.commit() is wrapped in an IntegrityError catch that replays the winner via ux_receivings_client_uuid — a unique index on the receivings table, which a failed REINDEX/CONCURRENTLY build on stock_batches cannot degrade. The losing retry's duplicate stock_batches roll back with its transaction, so stock/debt are not doubled. A retry without client_uuid creates a separate document even with all indexes healthy, so that is not an index-degradation defect. (2) Corrections (ux_recv_corr_client): apps/server/app/services/lot_correction.py _correct_once takes Purchase with_for_update() and re-runs the _replay client_uuid dedup UNDER that lock; the second concurrent request blocks until the first commits, then replays the first response. This serialization is lock-based and works with the index invalid; the outer correct() loop also catches IntegrityError -> _replay. (3) Shortfall resolutions (ux_lsr_request_client): apps/server/app/services/lot_resolution.py resolve has the identical pattern — fast dedup (line 301), with_for_update() locks (326-362), dedup re-run under lock (339-342), IntegrityError -> _replay (404-411). (4) ux_smove_alloc/ux_ret_alloc_line rows are per-parent-document children; duplicating them requires duplicating the parent movement/return, which is deduped at the parent level — the index is defense-in-depth, not the sole race barrier. Additional premise error: a failed CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY typically leaves indisvalid=false with indisready=true, and a ready unique index still raises 23505 on new inserts; the suggested repro (UPDATE pg_index SET indisvalid=false) leaves indisready=true, so the race would still be blocked. Only an indisready=false index enforces nothing, narrowing the window further. Caveat for the report (a DIFFERENT finding, not the one under test): /receiving/commit has no under-lock dedup recheck, so its sole race barrier is ux_receivings_client_uuid itself — an IDEMPOTENCY_INDEXES soft-class index with no require_index guard; degrading THAT index (indisready=false) would make the double-receiving race statically live. The finding as stated, targeting ux_lot_intake_key/ux_recv_corr_client/ux_lsr_request_client/ux_smove_alloc/ux_ret_alloc_line, is refuted.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Two index-independent or cross-table mechanisms: (a) apps/server/app/api/v1/receiving.py _commit_once — atomic transaction whose db.commit() catches IntegrityError from ux_receivings_client_uuid (receivings table, unaffected by stock_batches index degradation) and returns duplicate:true, rolling back the loser's duplicate stock_batches; (b) lock+recheck serialization in apps/server/app/services/lot_correction.py (_correct_once: Purchase with_for_update() then _replay re-run under lock) and apps/server/app/services/lot_resolution.py (resolve: with_for_update() then _replay re-run at lines 339-342), which dedups concurrent client_uuid retries without relying on the unique index.
verdicts.repro_hint: To probe the real residual seam (separate finding): on PG set ux_receivings_client_uuid to indisready=false AND indisvalid=false (or drop/recreate it as a plain non-unique index with the same name — boot stays green per required_schema soft classification), then send two concurrent identical POST /receiving/commit payloads with the same client_uuid and same supplier_id; since _commit_once never re-runs its client_uuid dedup after acquiring the Supplier FOR UPDATE lock, assert two receivings/purchases and doubled stock_batches. The five indexes named in the finding under test will not reproduce a double-write this way.

findings.title: index_guard verifies on a separate connection with a 10s stale-OK cache keyed on id(bind) — the guard never runs in the write transaction and the key can alias a disposed engine
findings.claim: require_index(db,...) resolves the bind via db.get_bind() (an Engine in production) and rs._unique_index_states opens a NEW pooled connection (_con_of: bind.connect()), so the catalog check is a different transaction from the guarded write; on top of that an OK verdict is cached for SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL=10s keyed on (id(bind), index, table). An index dropped or invalidated after a cached OK admits unguarded financial writes for up to TTL + in-flight transaction time. Additionally id() of a garbage-collected Engine can be reused by a new Engine object, so within one TTL window a fresh bind can be served the previous engine's cached verdict for a different database (test harnesses and multi-tenant probes create/dispose engines; the cache comment claims bind-scoping prevents exactly this cross-DB bleed).
findings.invariant: A guard verdict must be attributable to the same database (and ideally the same transaction snapshot) as the write it authorizes.
findings.attack_scenario: T0: payment request verifies ux_subpay_client_uuid, OK cached. T0+2s: operator DROP INDEX (or CONCURRENTLY rebuild leaves it invalid). T0+3s..T0+10s: two duplicate record_payment retries with the same client_uuid pass the guard from cache; the subscription-row lock serializes them but the second's SELECT-dedup runs after the first COMMITTED so it is actually caught — the exposed window is the enrol/doc_seq savepoint-race paths, where two first-allocations both pass the cached guard and, with the index gone, both INSERT DocCounter rows: duplicate receipt numbers. The stale-cache window is acknowledged in the module ('ESKIRGAN MUSBAT JAVOB OYNASI'), the id() aliasing is not.
findings.evidence: index_guard.py: _cache key '(id(bind), index, table)'; _TTL_SECONDS; _bind_of returns db.get_bind(); required_schema._con_of opens bind.connect() for an Engine. Comment claims 'KALIT BIND'NI HAM O'Z ICHIGA OLADI... Bindsiz kalit bir bazaning javobini boshqasiga qo'llardi' — id() reuse defeats this for up to TTL after engine disposal.
findings.suggested_repro: Python: create engine A, warm cache with BAD; dispose A; loop creating engines until id() matches; observe index_state returns cached BAD for the new healthy DB within 10s (or OK for an unhealthy one in the inverse setup).

verdicts.reasoning:
The finding's factual observations are accurate (guard runs on a pooled catalog connection separate from the write transaction; OK verdicts cached 10s keyed on (id(bind), index, table)), but every concrete financial-corruption path it needs is blocked by an independent protective mechanism at SHA 85be3991, and the id() aliasing has no production trigger.

1) id() aliasing is unreachable in production. The server process creates exactly one module-level Engine at import (apps/server/app/db/session.py:44, `engine = create_engine(_url, **_engine_kw)`) and never disposes it; every Session comes from that bind, so `db.get_bind()` returns the same long-lived object and its id() is stable for the process lifetime. The only other `create_engine` calls in app code (apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py, apps/server/app/tools/schema_migrate.py) run in separate CLI processes with their own `_cache`. Engine churn exists only in test harnesses, which are given `index_guard.reset_cache()` and whose suite explicitly tests bind isolation (apps/server/tests/test_index_guarantee_guard.py, cross-bind test at lines 122-126). No production financial write can be served an aliased verdict.

2) The 10s stale-OK window (which the module documents as a deliberate owner tradeoff, tunable via SAVDOOS_INDEX_GUARD_TTL down to 0) does not admit persisted corruption on any of the three guarded writers, because each has a second, independent constraint the attack scenario does not remove:
   - record_payment (apps/server/app/services/subscription/payments.py): the subscription row is locked FOR NO KEY UPDATE *before* the (company_id, client_uuid) dedup SELECT ("AVVAL QULF, KEYIN IDEMPOTENTLIK"). Duplicate retries serialize on the row lock; the loser re-reads under lock and returns the winner's committed payment. The finding itself concedes this path "is actually caught". ux_subpay_client_uuid is documented as the last barrier, not the first.
   - doc_seq (apps/server/app/services/doc_seq.py, `allocate`): the claimed outcome "duplicate receipt numbers" is blocked by document-level unique constraints that are separate objects from ux_doc_counter: Sale `UniqueConstraint("company_id","receipt_no")` (apps/server/app/models/sales.py:16), Return `UNIQUE(company_id, return_no)` (sales.py:160), Purchase `UNIQUE(company_id, doc_no)` (apps/server/app/models/purchasing.py:27), all present in live DDL (db/schema.sql:402, :640, :709). If ux_doc_counter is gone and two first-allocations both seed the same number inside their sale transactions, the second committer violates the receipt-level UNIQUE and its entire transaction — including its duplicate DocCounter row — rolls back. Neither a duplicate receipt number nor a duplicate counter row persists.
   - enrol (apps/server/app/services/subscription/lifecycle.py): with ux_subscriptions_company dropped, two parallel enrols within the stale window could persist two subscription rows, but the consequence is state.py's one_or_none() raising — a fail-closed denial for that tenant, not a financial loss (no double charge, no duplicate payment, append-only ledgers untouched). Reaching even that requires an operator DROP of a required production index (which turns /health/ready RED) plus two concurrent enrols of the same company by a platform admin inside a 10-second window — not a concrete attack, and squarely inside the residual window the module documents.

The guard is defense-in-depth layered on top of these constraints; its acknowledged TTL window never becomes the sole barrier for a write whose corruption would persist. The novel part of the finding (id() reuse) is refuted by the single-engine production topology; the rest restates a documented, bounded tradeoff.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: (a) Single module-level production Engine (apps/server/app/db/session.py:44) — id(bind) cannot alias in the server process. (b) record_payment locks the subscription row FOR NO KEY UPDATE before the dedup SELECT (payments.py steps 1-2), serializing duplicates independently of ux_subpay_client_uuid. (c) Document-level unique constraints UNIQUE(company_id, receipt_no)/(company_id, return_no)/(company_id, doc_no) (db/schema.sql:640/:709/:402; models sales.py:16,:160, purchasing.py:27) abort the losing transaction wholesale, preventing duplicate receipt numbers and duplicate DocCounter rows even with ux_doc_counter absent. (d) enrol residual degrades to state.py one_or_none() failure — fail-closed denial, not financial corruption.
verdicts.repro_hint: If the enrol residual is to be exercised anyway (PG required): drop ux_subscriptions_company, warm the cache with one enrol-path index_state OK, then race two enrol(commit=True) calls for the same company_id within 10s; observe two subscription rows and subsequent state.py one_or_none() raising (denial, not duplicate money). The id() aliasing repro only works by constructing engine churn absent from the server process.

findings.title: lifecycle.enrol maps every IntegrityError from the subscription INSERT to SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS — FK/CHECK violations report a subscription that does not exist
findings.claim: The except IntegrityError around db.flush([sub]) (:352-356) is meant for the ux_subscriptions_company race, but it also catches FK violations (company_id soft-deleted-then-purged or bogus, plan_id row deleted between plan_terms and flush) and any ck_sub_* CHECK failure, converting them to the stable refusal code SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS. A vendor billing tool that treats that code as 'company is enrolled' will skip the company permanently: per the module's own contract an un-enrolled tenant is grandfathered and never auto-restricted (state.py), i.e. it runs unbilled forever with no error surfacing.
findings.invariant: A duplicate-key refusal code must only be emitted for the duplicate-key constraint; other integrity failures must surface as errors so the enrolment is retried/investigated.
findings.attack_scenario: Platform admin enrols company X concurrently with the plan being deleted (or with a company row hard-removed by admin tooling); flush raises an FK IntegrityError; caller receives SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS with rollback; automation records X as enrolled; no subscription row exists; X is never restricted or billed and the state is only discoverable by manual audit.
findings.evidence: lifecycle.py:352-356: 'except IntegrityError as e: raise _refuse(db, LifecycleRefused("SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS", ...)' — no inspection of the violated constraint name, unlike cashops.py:163 which explicitly narrows ('ATAYLAB TOR TEKSHIRUV. Ilgari bu blok HAR QANDAY IntegrityError'ni "duplicate" deb...' — the codebase already learned this lesson elsewhere).
findings.suggested_repro: On PG: call lifecycle.enrol with a plan_id you delete after plan_terms via a second session (or a company_id with no companies row); observe SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS instead of an FK error, and subscriptions containing no row.

verdicts.reasoning: The company_id FK leg of the finding is provable by reading code alone; the CHECK leg is refuted; the plan_id leg is real but requires out-of-band DB surgery. Details: (1) apps/server/app/models/subscription.py defines Subscription.company_id with ForeignKey("companies.id") and plan_id with ForeignKey("plans.id") — real FKs enforced on PostgreSQL. (2) In apps/server/app/services/subscription/lifecycle.py, enrol() validates nothing about the company: _lock() only queries the subscriptions table and returns None equally for 'no subscription yet' and 'company row absent'; require_index() only checks that ux_subscriptions_company exists; _assert_owner() checks session hygiene. So an enrol call with a company_id not present in companies (typo'd UUID, or a row hard-removed by purge tooling) passes every pre-check, reaches db.flush([sub]) at :352, raises an FK IntegrityError, and the bare `except IntegrityError` at :353-356 unconditionally emits the stable refusal code SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS with rollback — reporting a subscription that does not exist. No concurrency or race is needed for this leg. (3) The plan_id FK leg is narrowed but not closed: plan_terms() raises PLAN_NOT_FOUND if the plans row is missing at query time, so only a concurrent hard DELETE of the plans row between that SELECT and the flush fires the FK; no app code path hard-deletes plans at this SHA (Plan is FullMixin soft-delete, no plan CRUD API), so this leg needs manual DB intervention. (4) The ck_sub_* CHECK leg of the finding is REFUTED: enrol inserts status=ACTIVE, restricted_at=None, cancelled_at=None, deleted_at=None, which satisfies ck_sub_deleted_never, ck_sub_restricted_iff, ck_sub_cancelled_iff, and ck_sub_status_persistable (apps/server/app/core/subscription_check_defs.py) by construction; the admin_audit_log insert (_audit) happens after the try block, so ck_audit_sub_fields failures surface as raw errors, correctly. (5) The codebase itself documents this exact anti-pattern as a previously fixed bug: apps/server/app/api/v1/cashops.py:163-175 ('ATAYLAB TOR TEKSHIRUV...') re-queries after IntegrityError and only claims duplicate when a matching row is confirmed to exist; lifecycle.enrol lacks that post-error confirmation. Impact mitigation: at SHA 85be3991 enrol has no HTTP route caller (git grep shows only tests/test_subscription_* reference it), so the 'vendor billing tool skips the company forever' scenario is prospective — it becomes live only when the admin enrolment route ships. Severity P2 with that caveat is fair; the fix is one confirming re-query (does a live subscription row for this company actually exist?) inside the except block, mirroring cashops.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial only: plan_terms() (lifecycle.py:289-301) pre-verifies the plans row exists, narrowing the plan_id FK leg to out-of-band hard deletes; and enrol's inserted values satisfy all ck_sub_* CHECKs by construction, closing the CHECK leg. Nothing protects the company_id FK leg — no company-existence check exists anywhere in enrol, _lock, _assert_owner, or require_index.
verdicts.repro_hint: On PostgreSQL (SQLite test DB also enforces FK here via PRAGMA foreign_keys per tests/test_subscription_lifecycle.py:45): create a plan, then call lifecycle.enrol(db, company_id=uuid.uuid4() (no companies row), plan_id=plan.id, months=1, actor=ACTOR, reason="x"). Expect LifecycleRefused with code SUBSCRIPTION_ALREADY_EXISTS despite SELECT count(*) FROM subscriptions WHERE company_id=<that uuid> returning 0. A correct implementation would surface the FK error (or a distinct COMPANY_NOT_FOUND).

findings.title: record_payment with client_uuid=None has zero idempotency on an append-only, uncorrectable payment registry
findings.claim: find_by_client_uuid returns None when client_uuid is None, and ux_subpay_client_uuid is partial (WHERE client_uuid IS NOT NULL), so a NULL-key payment has neither SELECT-dedup nor DB barrier: every retry writes a new SubscriptionPayment row AND extends current_period_end again. The module's own docstring states the table is deliberately append-only with no storno writer ('buni keyin TUZATIB BO'LMAYDI'), so a doubled manual payment is permanent in the registry. The guard require_index(:70-72) runs and passes — giving false assurance on a code path the index cannot protect.
findings.invariant: Every writer of an append-only money registry must be idempotent, or must refuse inputs for which its idempotency key is absent.
findings.attack_scenario: Vendor admin tool (future HTTP wiring, or a script using the library today) records a manual payment without generating client_uuid; the HTTP call times out after commit; the tool retries; the tenant's period is extended twice for one payment (revenue loss for the vendor) and the registry permanently shows two payments — the exact double-write the surrounding machinery exists to prevent, silently allowed by a nullable key.
findings.evidence: payments.py:33-36: 'if client_uuid is None: return None'; SubscriptionPayment(:101-108) inserts with client_uuid=None; no code path requires client_uuid to be non-null; index def required_schema.py:425 'WHERE client_uuid IS NOT NULL'.
findings.suggested_repro: Call payments.record_payment twice with client_uuid=None, same amount/reference; assert two rows in subscription_payments and current_period_end advanced by 2*months.

verdicts.reasoning: Every load-bearing claim checks out at the audited SHA, and no protective mechanism covers the NULL-key path. (1) apps/server/app/services/subscription/payments.py, find_by_client_uuid: `if client_uuid is None: return None` — the under-lock dedup lookup (step 2 of record_payment) is a no-op for NULL keys, so `existing` is always None and execution falls through to the INSERT and period extension. (2) The DB barrier is partial: apps/server/app/initdb.py:656-659 creates `ux_subpay_client_uuid ... WHERE client_uuid IS NOT NULL`, matching models/subscription.py:147-148 (`postgresql_where=_CLIENT_UUID_SET`); a row with client_uuid=NULL is outside the index predicate, so no unique violation is possible (and PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct in unique indexes anyway). (3) `client_uuid` is nullable=True on the model (models/subscription.py:171) and record_payment's signature explicitly types it `uuid.UUID | None`; git grep at the SHA shows no code path that refuses None — no validation, no CheckConstraint, no test asserting refusal. (4) index_guard.require_index (payments.py:70-72) verifies the index exists and is unique with the right columns/predicate — it says nothing about whether the current row falls under the predicate, so it passes on this path exactly as the finding says. (5) The row lock (lc._lock, FOR NO KEY UPDATE) only serializes the two calls; serialized or not, both see no existing payment and both write. renewal_base then computes the second base from the already-extended subscription, so current_period_end advances twice for one payment. (6) The registry is append-only at this SHA: SubscriptionPayment has a `reversal_of_id` column (models/subscription.py:168) but grep finds no storno writer anywhere in apps/server/app — the module's own comment confirms 'storno yozuvchisi YO'Q ... TUZATIB BO'LMAYDI'. The broken path (two calls with client_uuid=None → two rows + double extension) is provable from Python control flow plus the DDL alone; no runtime test is needed. Mitigating context for the report: at this SHA record_payment has no production caller — grep shows only tests invoke it (no HTTP route/admin wiring exists yet), so this is a latent library defect whose real-world trigger requires future wiring or a script that omits the key; the finding itself scopes the attack that way. P2 with that contingency is fair; the fix (refuse client_uuid=None, fail-closed like the module's other gates) is consistent with the module's stated design.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None for the NULL-key path. All four existing mechanisms — the FOR NO KEY UPDATE subscription row lock, the under-lock SELECT dedup (find_by_client_uuid), the partial unique index ux_subpay_client_uuid (WHERE client_uuid IS NOT NULL), and index_guard.require_index — protect only rows where client_uuid IS NOT NULL. There is no NOT NULL constraint, no validation refusing None, no CHECK tying client_uuid to non-storno rows, and no test locking a refusal. The only mitigant is circumstantial: no production caller of record_payment exists at this SHA (library-only exposure).
verdicts.repro_hint: Call app.services.subscription.payments.record_payment twice with the same company_id, client_uuid=None, months=1 (any amount/reference). Assert: (a) SELECT count(*) FROM subscription_payments WHERE company_id=... returns 2; (b) subscriptions.current_period_end advanced by 2 months total; (c) both calls returned created=True. Contrast with the same two calls using a shared uuid4() key, where the second returns (existing, False).

findings.title: /sync/push dead-letters paid offline sales on unclassified transient DB errors (InterfaceError, pool TimeoutError, ambiguous COMMIT failure)
findings.claim: The per-sale error taxonomy in push() marks only HTTPException(409/5xx) and sqlalchemy OperationalError as transient (retry:true). The final `except Exception` handler (sync.py:84-87) returns {"ok": false, "error": "server"} with NO retry flag, which per the QA OFF-1 contract the client treats as PERMANENT dead-letter. But several genuinely transient failures are NOT OperationalError in SQLAlchemy's hierarchy: sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError (sibling of DatabaseError, raised by psycopg when a connection is already closed), sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError (QueuePool exhaustion, pool_timeout=30 in app/db/session.py), and InternalError. create_sale() commits internally (services/sales.py:732 `db.commit()`), so a connection lost between flush and COMMIT can surface as InterfaceError with the sale NOT recorded — the paid check is then permanently dropped from the retry outbox.
findings.invariant: A paid offline check must never leave the client outbox until the server has durably recorded it (owner rule 'no lost transactions'; docs/PURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_PHASE1.md §11.3 justifies the ux_doc_counter guard by exactly this dead-letter risk, choosing 409 because it is transient).
findings.attack_scenario: Cashier sells offline, POS pushes the batch. During create_sale for one check, the PG backend/network dies at the wrong moment; the session raises sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError (not OperationalError) on the next statement or on COMMIT. push() falls into the bare `except Exception`, replies ok:false without retry, the client dead-letters the record. The sale was rolled back server-side: money was taken from the customer but no sale, no stock decrement and no cash-ledger leg ever exist. Same path fires for pool TimeoutError under load bursts.
findings.evidence: sync.py:83-87: `except Exception: db.rollback(); results.append({"client_uuid": ..., "ok": False, "error": "server"})` — no "retry" key, versus the HTTPException branch which computes `_transient` and the OperationalError branch which hardcodes retry:True. SQLAlchemy hierarchy: DBAPIError -> InterfaceError | DatabaseError -> OperationalError, so InterfaceError and pool TimeoutError bypass both transient branches. Minimal fix: add `except (sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError, sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError)` -> retry:true, and in a generic DBAPIError branch treat `e.connection_invalidated` as transient; keep DataError permanent.
findings.suggested_repro: TestClient against Postgres: monkeypatch Session.commit inside create_sale to raise sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError once (or pg_terminate_backend the session's PID mid-request); assert the push result row has ok:false and no retry:true although nothing was committed.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not; every link in the chain is provable by reading code at SHA 85be3991.

(1) Server taxonomy gap is real. apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py push(): the HTTPException branch computes `_transient = e.status_code >= 500 or e.status_code == 409` and returns a `retry` key; the `except OperationalError` branch hardcodes `retry: True`; the final `except Exception` branch returns only `{"client_uuid":..., "ok": False, "error": "server"}` — no `retry` key. Its own comment says it is intended for PERMANENT errors like DataError ("Numeric overflow, PERMANENT").

(2) The exception hierarchy claim is confirmed against the project's installed SQLAlchemy (apps/server/.venv/Lib/site-packages/sqlalchemy/exc.py): `class TimeoutError(SQLAlchemyError)` (line 288) and `class InterfaceError(DBAPIError)` (line 723) — neither is a subclass of `OperationalError(DatabaseError)` (line 741). Both bypass the transient branch and land in the bare `except Exception`.

(3) The TimeoutError path is concretely reachable per-sale, not only per-request. apps/server/app/db/session.py configures QueuePool with `pool_timeout=30` for Postgres, and its own comment admits "yuqori konkurentlikда QueuePool timeout -> 500". create_sale commits internally (apps/server/app/services/sales.py:731 `db.commit()`), which releases the connection back to the pool at each loop iteration; the next sale's first query re-checks out a connection, and under pool exhaustion that checkout raises sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError from INSIDE the per-sale try — a genuinely transient load-burst error that gets answered ok:false with no retry flag.

(4) The client really dead-letters on that answer. packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts flushOutbox(): `if (r.ok) outboxRemove(...) else if (r.retry) { keep } else if (deadLetter(i, ...)) outboxRemove(i.client_uuid)`. So ok:false without retry removes the paid check from the retry outbox permanently.

(5) Protective mechanisms hunted, none refutes: (a) client_uuid idempotency in _create_sale_once only helps if a retry happens — dead-letter guarantees it never does; (b) `pool_pre_ping=True` only validates connections at checkout, and does nothing for pool TimeoutError; (c) create_sale's internal 3x retry covers only IntegrityError (escalating to 409, which IS transient) — not these classes; (d) the QA OFF-3 dead-letter list (localStorage `savdoos_outbox_failed`) makes the loss VISIBLE ("N rad etildi" badge, packages/shared/src/screens/POSKassa.tsx ~700-745) but the dialog offers only Close and Clear — there is no resubmit path, so the sale (money already taken from the customer) is never recorded server-side: no Sale row, no stock decrement, no cash-ledger leg.

The one softening versus the finding text: the check is not silently lost — the cashier sees a rejected-sales badge with the amount and could manually re-ring it. But the stated invariant ("a paid offline check must never leave the client outbox until the server has durably recorded it") is violated for genuinely transient failures, exactly the risk docs cite to justify treating 409 as transient. The InterfaceError sub-claim is slightly weaker (psycopg3 maps most connection loss to OperationalError, which IS caught; InterfaceError arises mainly when operating on an already-closed connection), but pool TimeoutError alone fully proves the defect.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial mitigations only, none sufficient: client_uuid idempotency in _create_sale_once (apps/server/app/services/sales.py) — inert once the client stops retrying; pool_pre_ping=True (apps/server/app/db/session.py) — checkout-time only, does not cover pool TimeoutError or mid-transaction loss; QA OFF-3 dead-letter visibility (packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts deadLetter + POSKassa.tsx failed dialog) — makes the drop visible to the cashier but offers no resubmission, only Clear.
verdicts.repro_hint: Static proof suffices, but a runtime demo: TestClient on Postgres, monkeypatch sqlalchemy.pool.QueuePool._do_get (or Session.connection) to raise sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError once during the second sale of a 2-sale /sync/push batch; assert results[1] == {"ok": False, "error": "server"} with no "retry" key and that no Sale row exists for that client_uuid — then assert the shared-client contract (sync.ts) would call deadLetter/outboxRemove for that shape.

verdicts.reasoning: The defect is provable by reading code at 85be3991. Server side (apps/server/app/api/v1/sync.py, push): only two transient-aware handlers exist — `except HTTPException` (retry = status>=500 or ==409) and `except OperationalError` (retry:True); the final bare `except Exception` appends {"ok": False, "error": "server"} with NO retry key. Client side (packages/shared/src/lib/sync.ts, flushOutbox): a result with ok falsy and retry falsy is dead-lettered via deadLetter() and then outboxRemove() — and the dead-letter list has no requeue path anywhere (POSKassa.tsx failed-sales modal offers only clearFailed()). So any per-sale exception outside those two classes permanently removes a paid offline check from the retry queue. At least one genuinely transient, definitely-not-recorded failure reaches that bare except: sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError from QueuePool checkout (pool_timeout=30 configured in apps/server/app/db/session.py for Postgres; that file's own comment acknowledges QueuePool timeout under high concurrency). Because create_sale commits per sale (apps/server/app/services/sales.py:731) and SessionLocal releases the connection at transaction end, every subsequent sale in a batch re-checks-out a connection inside the loop; under pool saturation that checkout raises TimeoutError inside the per-sale try before any statement runs — the sale is certainly not recorded, yet the client dead-letters it. sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError subclasses SQLAlchemyError, not OperationalError, and sqlalchemy.exc.InterfaceError sits beside DatabaseError under DBAPIError — neither is caught, exactly as the finding states. CAVEAT correcting one leg of the claim: the driver is psycopg v3 (postgresql+psycopg in session.py), which raises OperationalError (not InterfaceError) for connections lost during execution or COMMIT; that path IS caught with retry:True and the retry is safe because create_sale is idempotent on client_uuid (services/sales.py:59-61). So the dramatized "InterfaceError between flush and COMMIT" scenario is unlikely with this driver, and the ambiguous-COMMIT case is actually handled. The confirmed broken path is the unclassified-transient gap itself, with pool TimeoutError as the concrete, codebase-acknowledged trigger (InterfaceError on an already-closed/invalidated connection is a rarer secondary trigger). Severity stands: a paid offline sale is silently (from the retry queue's perspective) converted into a localStorage-only failed entry with no server record, no stock decrement, no cash-ledger leg, and no resubmission mechanism.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial protections exist but do not cover the confirmed path: (1) pool_pre_ping=True in app/db/session.py recycles stale connections at checkout, but does nothing for pool exhaustion (TimeoutError) since that is a queue wait, not a dead connection; (2) psycopg v3 maps mid-statement/COMMIT connection loss to OperationalError, which push() does catch with retry:True, and create_sale's client_uuid idempotency lookup makes that retry safe — this neutralizes the finding's headline InterfaceError-on-COMMIT scenario but not the TimeoutError/InterfaceError taxonomy gap; (3) dead-letter is not fully silent — the cashier sees a "failed" badge and the list persists in localStorage — but the only UI action is clearFailed() (delete), so recovery requires manually re-ringing the sale.
verdicts.repro_hint: No dynamic test needed for confirmation, but a demonstrating test: TestClient POST /sync/push with one offline sale, monkeypatching app.services.sales.create_sale (or Session's connection checkout) to raise sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError("QueuePool limit") once; assert the result row is {"ok": false, "error": "server"} with no "retry" key, while a control raising sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError yields retry:true. Then feed that row shape to flushOutbox's handling (or unit-test the branch) to show outboxRemove is called. Fix direction matches the finding: catch sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError and InterfaceError as retry:true, and in a generic DBAPIError branch treat e.connection_invalidated as transient while keeping DataError/IntegrityError permanent.

findings.title: index_guard cache keyed by id(bind): verdicts can leak between different databases after engine GC reuses the id
findings.claim: The module-global cache uses key `(id(bind), index, table)` (index_guard.py:76 `_cache`, :91 `key = (id(bind), index, table)`) and holds no reference to the bind. CPython reuses id() addresses as soon as an object is collected, so if engine A (database A, verdict OK cached) is disposed and a new engine B for a different database is allocated at the same address within the 10s TTL, a guarded write on B is approved (or refused) using A's verdict — the guard 'proves' an index it never inspected on that database. The code comment explicitly claims the bind in the key prevents cross-database mixing ('Bindsiz kalit bir bazaning javobini boshqasiga qo'llardi') — that guarantee does not actually hold across engine lifetimes, and the docstring itself anticipates multi-database processes ('ko'p-tenant zondlari').
findings.invariant: A cached OK for (bind, index, table) must only ever be served for the exact database the catalog was read from.
findings.attack_scenario: A probe/maintenance loop (or the test suite) creates short-lived engines per tenant DB: engine A for a healthy tenant caches OK for ux_doc_counter; A is GC'd; engine B is created for a tenant whose ux_doc_counter is invalid and lands on the same id; within 10s a doc_seq.allocate through B returns OK without any catalog read, and the write proceeds against a database with no counter-uniqueness guarantee. Production single-engine deployments are unaffected, which is also why no test catches it.
findings.evidence: index_guard.py:76 `_cache: dict[tuple[int, str, str], tuple[float, str]]`; :91 `key = (id(bind), index, table)`; nothing keeps `bind` alive. test_BIND_boyicha_ALOHIDA_keshlanadi only proves separation while both binds are alive. Minimal fix: store the cache on the bind itself (e.g. a dict attached to the Engine) or key via weakref.ref(bind) so entries die with the engine.
findings.suggested_repro: Pure-Python: cache OK for a _FakeBind, del it, allocate new objects until id() repeats, show index_state returns the stale verdict without calling _unique_index_states.

verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Process-lifetime module-global engine: `apps/server/app/db/session.py:44` (`engine = create_engine(_url, **_engine_kw)`) is held forever by the module attribute and by `SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, ...)` (session.py:72). Every bind that ever reaches `index_state` is this one object, so it can never be garbage-collected and its `id()` can never be reused. Additionally, even under a hypothetical id collision, a stale BAD/UNVERIFIABLE verdict errs fail-closed (409 refusal), so only a stale OK is dangerous — and that path requires a multi-engine caller that does not exist at this SHA.
verdicts.reasoning: The claimed CPython behavior is accurate as an abstract hazard: `apps/server/app/core/index_guard.py` keys `_cache` on `(id(bind), index, table)` and keeps no reference to the bind, so id() reuse after GC could in principle serve a stale verdict. But the finding's attack cannot be made concrete against the audited codebase. (1) `require_index` has exactly three call sites at SHA 85be3991: `apps/server/app/services/doc_seq.py:146`, `apps/server/app/services/subscription/lifecycle.py:331`, and `apps/server/app/services/subscription/payments.py:71`. All three receive a FastAPI `db` session created by `get_db()` from `SessionLocal`, whose `Session.get_bind()` returns the single module-global engine (`apps/server/app/db/session.py:44`, held by the module namespace and by the sessionmaker closure for the life of the process). An object that is permanently referenced is never collected, so its id is never recycled — the precondition of the attack (engine A disposed, engine B allocated at the same address) is unreachable. (2) The postulated 'probe/maintenance loop creating short-lived engines per tenant DB' does not exist: multi-tenancy in this system is intra-database (company_id scoping in one Postgres DB), not engine-per-tenant. The only in-app code that creates additional engines is `apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py` and `apps/server/app/tools/schema_migrate.py`, and a git grep of `apps/server/app/tools` for index_guard/require_index/doc_seq returns nothing — those tools never touch the guard. (3) Test-suite exposure is not a financial-integrity path, and the guard tests call `ig.reset_cache()` around bind changes (`tests/test_index_guarantee_guard.py:28,30,152`, `tests/test_subscription_migration_pg.py:551-566`). (4) Directionally, half of the claimed failure ('or refused') is fail-safe: a leaked BAD/UNVERIFIABLE only over-refuses. The residual risk — a leaked OK — requires two live-then-dead engines to different databases inside one process within the 10s TTL, which no code at this SHA can produce. The finding is a legitimate latent-hardening suggestion (key via weakref.ref(bind) or store the cache on the engine), but as stated — a P2 verdict-leak between databases — it is refuted for lack of any reachable path.
verdicts.repro_hint: The suggested pure-Python repro (cache OK for a _FakeBind, delete it, allocate until id() repeats) would demonstrate only the abstract CPython id-reuse property, not a defect reachable from any code path in apps/server at this SHA; to make the finding stand, the finder must exhibit an actual caller that creates and discards engines to different databases and reaches require_index within the 10s TTL.

findings.title: Expanding REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS to 8 entries breaks two exact-equality tests, so the guard-shape expansion at this SHA has never run green through CI
findings.claim: At 85be3991 REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS holds 8 names (ux_subscriptions_company, ux_subpay_client_uuid, ux_doc_counter, ux_print_jobs_original, ux_products_external_identity, ux_lot_intake_key, ux_lsr_request_client, ux_recv_corr_client). index_definition_states() returns an entry for every registered name found in the database, and both test DBs are built by a full initdb which creates all 8 indexes on both dialects. Yet test_subscription_migration_pg.py:394-397 and test_subscription_lifecycle.py:975-978 (test_SQLITE_majburiy_indeks_tariflari_TOGRI) assert `st == {"ux_subscriptions_company": IX_DEF_OK, "ux_subpay_client_uuid": IX_DEF_OK}` — an exact 2-key equality that now fails with 8 keys. So at this snapshot the suite is red, and more importantly no green CI run has ever proven that the six newly registered shapes (notably ux_doc_counter, guarding EVERY sale/return/purchase number) evaluate IX_DEF_OK against a real initdb-built Postgres catalog; a canon/definition mismatch there would 409 every document-number write in production.
findings.invariant: Every shape registered in REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS must be proven IX_DEF_OK on an initdb-built database by a passing test before the fail-closed guard that consumes it ships.
findings.attack_scenario: The snapshot is merged with the two tests skipped/ignored as 'known red'; if any of the six new shape tuples disagrees with what Postgres actually stores for the initdb DDL (the ux_subpay incident in the file header shows this exact class happened before), index_state returns BAD for a healthy index and doc_seq.allocate refuses every sale storewide with SCHEMA_GUARANTEE_MISSING.
findings.evidence: required_schema.py REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS: 8 keys (verified by grep). index_definition_states: 'Faqat TOPILGANLARI' — returns all found registered names. test_subscription_migration_pg.py:394: `assert st == {"ux_subscriptions_company": rs.IX_DEF_OK, "ux_subpay_client_uuid": rs.IX_DEF_OK}, st`. Minimal fix: change both asserts to subset/superset form (assert every registered name maps to IX_DEF_OK) so they also cover the six new shapes.
findings.suggested_repro: Run pytest tests/test_subscription_lifecycle.py::test_SQLITE_majburiy_indeks_tariflari_TOGRI at this SHA (SQLite, no PG needed): the equality assert fails with an 8-key dict.

verdicts.reasoning: Every link of the claim verifies by direct read at 85be3991. (1) apps/server/app/core/required_schema.py:997-1028 REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS holds exactly 8 names. (2) required_schema.index_definition_states has no 2-key filter: the PG branch queries pg_index with relname = ANY(sorted(REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS)) and the SQLite branch iterates all 8 registry entries, skipping only names absent from sqlite_master. (3) Both test DBs are built by full initdb (test_subscription_migration_pg.py _initdb(url); test_subscription_lifecycle.py _sqlite_boot runs `python -m app.initdb`), and apps/server/app/initdb.py::_ensure_indexes creates all six new indexes via _index (initdb.py:351), which executes on BOTH dialects (the PG-only part is just the lock-free precheck); ux_lsr_request_client, ux_recv_corr_client and ux_print_jobs_original are also model-declared unique Indexes (models/inventory.py:379, receiving.py:57, receipt.py:74), so create_all builds them on a fresh DB regardless. Hence st has 8 keys on both dialects. (4) test_subscription_migration_pg.py:395-396 (test_PG_MAJBURIY_indekslar_TAYYORLIKDA_talab_qilinadi) and test_subscription_lifecycle.py:976-977 (test_SQLITE_majburiy_indeks_tariflari_TOGRI) both assert `st == {"ux_subscriptions_company": rs.IX_DEF_OK, "ux_subpay_client_uuid": rs.IX_DEF_OK}` — exact equality that fails with an 8-key dict whatever the six new states are. No skip/xfail marker on either test, and the SQLite test runs without Postgres, so the ordinary CI path is red at this snapshot. No protective mechanism refutes it: nothing narrows st, nothing updates the asserts at this SHA. Consequence framing is correct: because the assert fails before proving anything, no green run at this SHA demonstrates the six new tuples (including ux_doc_counter, consumed fail-closed via doc_seq.py:146 require_index and index_guard.py:98-107 definition check) evaluate IX_DEF_OK on an initdb-built catalog; the file header documents this exact mismatch class occurring before on ux_subpay_client_uuid. Nuance: I compared the six registry tuples against _ensure_indexes DDL and they textually match (table, column order, predicate), so the storewide-409 attack is a contingent risk (canonicalization mismatch), not a demonstrated wrong shape — the confirmed defect is the red suite / unproven guard shapes, matching the P2 severity.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. index_definition_states returns all found registered names (8 after initdb on both dialects); both asserts are exact 2-key equality; neither test is skipped or xfailed; _index in initdb.py is not dialect-gated, so the SQLite test DB also contains the six new indexes.
verdicts.repro_hint: pytest apps/server/tests/test_subscription_lifecycle.py::test_SQLITE_majburiy_indeks_tariflari_TOGRI at 85be3991 (SQLite only): the equality assert at lines 976-977 fails, with the printed st showing 8 keys. Fix: change both asserts to verify every name in rs.REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS maps to rs.IX_DEF_OK (superset form), so the six new shapes are actually proven against an initdb-built catalog.

findings.title: Guard cache-miss opens extra catalog connections mid-transaction while holding row locks on the hottest write path (documented as the cause of the 7-guard suite collapse, cost remains for the kept 3)
findings.claim: For an Engine bind (the normal Session case), a cache miss in index_state runs rs._unique_index_states and, for registered names, rs.index_definition_states — each via _con_of(engine) -> `bind.connect()`, i.e. up to two additional pool checkouts. doc_seq.allocate calls the guard on every sale, and create_sale invokes it late (services/sales.py:663) after Inventory and Customer FOR NO KEY UPDATE locks are held. There is no single-flight: at every 10s TTL expiry all concurrent requests miss simultaneously. With pool_size 15 + max_overflow 25 (app/db/session.py), if concurrent requests hold all pool connections, the guard's checkout blocks up to pool_timeout=30s while the caller keeps inventory/counter locks, serializing the tenant, then raises sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError -> 500 — which finding 1 turns into a dead-lettered paid check on /sync/push. §11.3 of docs/PURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_PHASE1.md records that exactly this cost ('index_definition_states esa ALOHIDA ulanish ochadi') collapsed the cash test suite when 7 guards were wired; the mechanism is unchanged for the 3 kept guards.
findings.invariant: A guard on the hot money path must never require an additional pool connection while the request transaction holds row locks, or must degrade without blocking the write for unrelated pool pressure.
findings.attack_scenario: SaaS instance with many tenants: at a TTL boundary, N>=40 in-flight requests each hold their session connection; several sales miss the guard cache at once and each requests a 2nd (and 3rd, for the shape query) connection; checkouts queue 30s while inventory locks are held, stalling every sale of those tenants, then fail with TimeoutError; offline pushes among them are dead-lettered.
findings.evidence: index_guard.index_state -> rs._unique_index_states(bind,...) and rs.index_definition_states(bind), both using `with bind.connect()` (required_schema._con_of); doc_seq.allocate:146 guard call; sales.py:663 allocation after locks. Minimal fix without weakening the check: run the catalog SELECTs on the session's own connection (they are plain reads and _con_of already supports a Connection bind — pass db.connection() instead of the engine), and/or add a per-key single-flight lock so one prober refreshes the TTL for everyone.
findings.suggested_repro: PG: set DB_POOL_SIZE=1, DB_MAX_OVERFLOW=0, hold one connection open, call doc_seq.allocate with a fresh guard cache — the request blocks pool_timeout then raises TimeoutError while its transaction holds the session connection.

verdicts.reasoning: Core defect confirmed by reading the SHA; one escalation sub-claim is wrong. (1) Extra pool checkout while holding locks: production sessions are Engine-bound (apps/server/app/db/session.py:72 `SessionLocal = sessionmaker(bind=engine, ...)`), so `require_index(db,...)` -> `_bind_of(db)` = `db.get_bind()` = Engine, and `required_schema._con_of` (apps/server/app/core/required_schema.py:721) takes the `bind.connect()` branch — a fresh pool checkout, not the session's connection. On a cache miss `index_guard.index_state` runs `rs._unique_index_states(bind,...)` AND, because `ux_doc_counter` IS registered in `REQUIRED_INDEX_DEFINITIONS` (required_schema.py:1009), also `rs.index_definition_states(bind)` — two sequential extra checkouts (peak concurrent extra demand 1, since the first `with` closes before the second opens). (2) Lock ordering: `doc_seq.allocate` calls `require_index` at apps/server/app/services/doc_seq.py:146 before touching the counter, and `services/sales.py:663` calls allocate deliberately late ("commit'ga imkon qadar YAQIN") — after Inventory `with_for_update()` (sales.py:268/276/316) and Customer `with_for_update(key_share=True)` (sales.py:638). So the checkout is made while the transaction holds row locks. (3) No single-flight: `_cache` is a bare dict keyed by (id(bind), index, table); at every 10s TTL expiry (`_TTL_SECONDS`) all concurrent guarded writes miss together, and UNVERIFIABLE is never cached, so a failing probe is retried by every request. (4) Pool: pool_size 15 + max_overflow 25, pool_timeout 30 (session.py:38-43); with all 40 connections held by in-flight requests, the guard checkout blocks up to 30s while inventory/customer locks are held — a self-inflicted stall provable from the code, and §11.3 of docs/PURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_PHASE1.md (lines 655-661) explicitly records this exact cost ("index_definition_states esa ALOHIDA ulanish ochadi") as the cause of the 7-guard cash-suite collapse, with the mechanism unchanged for the 3 kept guards. HOWEVER the claimed tail "raises sqlalchemy.exc.TimeoutError -> 500 -> dead-lettered paid check" is REFUTED: both catalog calls sit inside `try/except Exception` in `index_state` (index_guard.py, the `_unique_index_states` call and the `index_definition_states` call each), so a pool TimeoutError is swallowed, returns UNVERIFIABLE (uncached), and `require_index` raises HTTPException 409 SCHEMA_GUARANTEE_MISSING — not a 500. §11.3's own kept-guard table states this 409 is treated as transient by the sync client ("409 esa tranzient -> outbox'da qoladi"), i.e. the paid check stays in the outbox and is retried, not dead-lettered. Net: real, statically provable P2 availability/latency defect (30s lock-holding stall + tenant-wide 409 burst at pool saturation on a TTL boundary), but the irreversible-money consequence does not follow.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial mitigations exist but none prevents the extra checkout: (a) `index_state` wraps both catalog probes in `except Exception -> UNVERIFIABLE`, converting a pool TimeoutError into a fail-closed 409 (SCHEMA_GUARANTEE_MISSING) instead of a 500 — and per docs/PURCHASE_SETTLEMENT_PHASE1.md §11.3 the sync client treats that 409 as transient, so the paid check remains in the outbox (no dead-letter); (b) OK/BAD results are cached 10s per engine, bounding probe frequency off TTL boundaries; (c) the two extra checkouts are sequential, so peak extra demand is one connection per request. Nothing prevents the checkout-while-holding-locks or provides single-flight: `_con_of` only reuses an existing connection when the bind IS a Connection, which never happens for the Engine-bound request sessions (session.py:72).
verdicts.repro_hint: PG only. Set DB_POOL_SIZE=1, DB_MAX_OVERFLOW=0. Open one raw `engine.connect()` and hold it. In a request-style Session (SessionLocal()), begin a transaction, take any row lock, call `index_guard.reset_cache()`, then `doc_seq.allocate(db, company_id, "SALE")`. Expected: the call blocks ~pool_timeout (30s) while the session's transaction (and its locks) stay open, then returns HTTP 409 SCHEMA_GUARANTEE_MISSING (not TimeoutError/500) because index_state catches the checkout timeout as UNVERIFIABLE. Verify the 409 is retryable on /sync/push (check stays in outbox, not dead-letter).

map.summary: RELEASE SAFETY area at 38f1d750 (P8.1) = e60c213a (P8 main) + one commit ("Make the deploy gate prove itself..."), touching only staging-deploy.yml, staging-backup.yml, RELEASE_SAFETY_RUNBOOK.md and two test files; _db-backup-core.yml, db-backup.yml, restore-rehearsal.yml, ci.yml, uptime.yml are byte-identical at both SHAs.
