findings.title: APPLY --commit accepts --no-sidecar: the 'test only' hash-sidecar bypass is not enforced on the write path
findings.claim: The apply subparser reuses bundle_args, which adds `--no-sidecar` (help text: "FAQAT test: yon fayl talab qilinmaydi"), and cmd_apply passes `require_sidecar=not a.no_sidecar` straight into load_file — including for `--commit`. Nothing restricts the flag to test/dev, so a committing migration can run against a bundle whose bytes were never checked against the externally recorded `.sha256`.
findings.invariant: The runbook chain (SANDBOX_RESTORE_RUNBOOK / FIRST_REAL_COPY_CHECKLIST) treats the sidecar as the tie between the export file and the administrator's written record; a committing apply should always verify it. A bypass documented as test-only must be unusable on the irreversible path.
findings.attack_scenario: Operator's bundle gets truncated/re-saved (e.g. editor or transfer re-encoding) after dry-run notes were taken; they lost the .sha256 and rerun `apply --commit --no-sidecar`. load_bytes computes file_sha256 of whatever bytes are present; if the operator also regenerated report/mapping from the altered file (the checklist steps are all re-runnable) the whole hash chain is self-consistent against the wrong bytes, and the only remaining out-of-band check is the manually typed --expect-plan-sha256, which the operator may copy from the regenerated plan.json.
findings.evidence: migrate_1c.py bundle_args: `p.add_argument("--no-sidecar", action="store_true", help="FAQAT test: yon fayl talab qilinmaydi")` is attached to the apply parser; cmd_apply: `bundle = load_file(a.bundle, a.sha256, require_sidecar=not a.no_sidecar)` with no `a.commit` guard. bundle.py load_file only raises when `require_sidecar` and the file is missing.
findings.suggested_repro: python -m app.tools.migrate_1c apply --bundle export.json --no-sidecar --report r.json --mapping m.json --expect-system-identifier <staging sysid> --actor-employee-id <uuid> --expect-plan-sha256 <sha> --commit  (no .sha256 present) — commit proceeds.

verdicts.reasoning: The unguarded path is provable by reading the code at 40150b54. In apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py, main() builds the `apply` subparser with `bundle_args(p)`, and bundle_args adds `p.add_argument("--no-sidecar", action="store_true", help="FAQAT test: yon fayl talab qilinmaydi")` (line 273). cmd_apply then does `bundle = load_file(a.bundle, a.sha256, require_sidecar=not a.no_sidecar)` (line 209) with no coupling to `a.commit` — the only commit-specific gate in cmd_apply is the mandatory `--expect-plan-sha256`. In apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/bundle.py, load_file (line 399) only raises BundleError for a missing sidecar when `require_sidecar` is true; with the flag, `expected=None` reaches load_bytes and the external-hash comparison (`expected_sha256 is not None`) is skipped entirely. So `apply --commit --no-sidecar` commits without ever tying the bundle bytes to an external record, while docs/FAYZAN_1C_DEPENDENCY_MATRIX.md (lines 120, 381) and FAYZAN_CUTOVER_RUNBOOK_DRAFT.md declare the `.json.sha256` sidecar MAJBURIY (mandatory) in the file-layer contract — confirming the invariant premise. I hunted for compensating protections and found real but incomplete ones, which narrow the exploit class without closing it: (1) strict_json_loads rejects floats/duplicate keys/NaN, so many re-saves fail to parse; (2) bundle.py _validate cross-checks manifest counts against actual file contents (line 305: "eksport to'liq emas yoki buzilgan"), so truncation or dropped rows are caught sidecar or not; (3) classify's reconciliation recomputes per-warehouse sums/price min-max/counts, and mapping.py build_plan line 195 refuses to build a plan when reconciliation is not ok — so an accidentally value-corrupted file cannot even produce the regenerated chain; (4) apply_migration recomputes the report from the actual bundle and raises DriftError on report_sha256 mismatch vs both reviewed report and mapping (apply.py:158-161), and the report embeds bundle.file_sha256 (classify.py:602), so a bundle differing from the one the reviewed report was made from is rejected; (5) freshness, AlreadyApplied and StaleSnapshotError bound replay of old exports. None of these, however, restricts --no-sidecar itself, and the finding's regeneration scenario defeats (4)-(5) because every link (report, mapping, plan, expect-plan-sha256) is recomputable from the wrong bytes. A concrete residual corruption class survives all internal checks: structure-preserving text corruption (e.g., UTF-8 double-encoding mojibake of product names during transfer — valid UTF-8, parses strictly, digits/sums/manifest untouched) would commit 7000+ garbled catalog names; only the external sidecar comparison would have caught it. Severity note for calibration: the sidecar defends against accidents, not attackers (a co-located .sha256 is regenerable by anyone who can alter the bundle), and the internal manifest/reconciliation gates already catch most accident classes — P2 is appropriate, not higher.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Partial only: strict JSON parsing + manifest count/sum cross-validation (apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/bundle.py _validate line ~305), build_plan's reconciliation gate (apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/mapping.py:195), apply's report_sha256 DriftError re-check and mandatory --expect-plan-sha256 for --commit (apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/apply.py:158-176, migrate_1c.py cmd_apply). These block truncation and most value corruption but nothing restricts --no-sidecar to non-commit runs, and the whole hash chain is regenerable from altered bytes.
verdicts.repro_hint: Static: git show 40150b54:apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py — bundle_args (adds --no-sidecar, attached to the apply parser) and cmd_apply line 209 (`require_sidecar=not a.no_sidecar`, no a.commit guard); bundle.py load_file:399-410 shows the skipped check. Dynamic (if ever needed, non-prod): run `apply --commit --no-sidecar` with report/mapping/plan regenerated from a bundle whose product name fields were double-encoded (valid UTF-8, manifest untouched) and no .sha256 present — commit proceeds.

findings.title: Any IntegrityError on the import-job claim flush is reported as AlreadyApplied ('parallel apply claimed this export')
findings.claim: apply.py:204-207 wraps the claim flush in a blanket `except IntegrityError: raise AlreadyApplied("parallel apply ayni eksportni egalladi")` without checking that the violated constraint is ux_import_jobs_snapshot. A different constraint failing at that flush (e.g. the created_by FK if the resolved employee row is concurrently hard-deleted, or any future check/enum constraint on import_jobs) is misreported as the export already being applied.
findings.invariant: Per the audit method, error handling around an idempotency constraint must attribute the violation to that constraint. AlreadyApplied is an operator-facing terminal verdict ("do not retry, it is done") and must only be raised when a committed/committing job for this snapshot actually exists.
findings.attack_scenario: An unrelated integrity failure fires on the ImportJob insert (schema drift on a staging clone, missing partial-index support, FK race on employees). The operator sees 'parallel apply claimed this export', concludes the migration is done or in someone else's hands, and skips the cutover; verify-applied later finds no job, but only if the operator thinks to run it — the runbook's happy path for AlreadyApplied is to stop.
findings.evidence: apply.py: `db.add(job); try: db.flush(); except IntegrityError as e: raise AlreadyApplied("parallel apply ayni eksportni egalladi") from e` — no inspection of e.orig / constraint name, unlike the 55P03 sqlstate check done for the company lock a few lines above.
findings.suggested_repro: On PG: drop or violate any other import_jobs constraint (e.g. point created_by at a nonexistent employee by deleting the row in a parallel session after resolve_actor), run apply — observe AlreadyApplied instead of the real error.

verdicts.reasoning:
The blanket `except IntegrityError` at apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/apply.py:204-207 is real and does not inspect the constraint name, but every concrete path by which a *different* constraint could fire at that flush is already blocked by existing mechanisms, and the one residual (out-of-band raw SQL) does not hide the real error from the operator.

Constraints on the `import_jobs` INSERT flushed there (the only pending object — everything before `db.add(job)` is reads/locks, and `resolve_actor` in migrator_1c/actor.py explicitly "Hech narsa yozmaydi"):
1. FK company_id -> companies: refuted by the row lock taken at apply.py:107-110 — the Company row is held `with_for_update(key_share=True)` (FOR NO KEY UPDATE) for the whole transaction, so a concurrent DELETE of that row (which needs FOR UPDATE) blocks until apply commits. Additionally the app never hard-deletes companies: `admin_delete_company` (apps/server/app/api/v1/admin.py, @router.delete("/companies/{company_id}")) only sets `deleted_at`.
2. FK created_by -> employees (the finding's main scenario): unreachable through the application. `delete_employee` (apps/server/app/api/v1/employees.py:501) sets `e.deleted_at = datetime.now(...)` — soft delete only; a repo-wide grep for `db.delete(` at the SHA shows no hard delete of Employee rows anywhere in app code. The FK can therefore only be violated by hand-written `DELETE FROM employees` SQL committed in the seconds between `resolve_actor` (which re-checks the row exists, is active, same company) and the flush — not an application race.
3. Enum drift on `import_jobs.status`: an unknown label on a PG native enum raises InvalidTextRepresentation -> sqlalchemy DataError, NOT IntegrityError, so it is not caught by this except and propagates as the real error.
4. The only unique index on import_jobs is `ux_import_jobs_snapshot` itself (initdb.py:640-644; required_schema.py:381 makes its existence a boot-fatal requirement, refuting the "index missing on a clone" branch — and if it were missing, no IntegrityError would fire at all, so nothing gets mislabeled). PK is uuid4. All NOT NULL columns are populated.
5. `mode`, `snapshot_id`, `content_sha256` are plain nullable String columns — no CHECK constraints exist on the table at this SHA.

Also, even in the residual manual-SQL scenario the invariant's consequence ("operator concludes it is done and stops") does not follow: the sole caller is the CLI `cmd_apply` (apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py:214-227), which catches BaseException, rolls back, and RE-RAISES — no handler anywhere converts AlreadyApplied into a friendly message (grep shows AlreadyApplied is referenced only inside apply.py in app code). Because line 207 uses `raise ... from e`, the operator's terminal prints the full chained traceback: the original `IntegrityError` with psycopg's constraint/FK name appears FIRST, followed by "The above exception was the direct cause of ... AlreadyApplied". The real violated constraint is therefore never hidden from the operator; only the final exception class is imprecise. Combined with the FOR NO KEY UPDATE company lock serializing all applies (so a genuine parallel apply is normally caught earlier, at apply.py:127, with the job id), the mislabeling requires an attack that cannot be made concrete within the application, and its worst-case observable output still names the true constraint. Cosmetic hygiene issue (constraint-name check would match the 55P03 pattern used at line 113), not a P2 integrity defect.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: (a) Company row lock `with_for_update(key_share=True)` at apply.py:107 held across the flush — blocks any concurrent delete/update of the FK-referenced companies row; (b) app-wide soft-delete-only for employees (api/v1/employees.py:501 sets deleted_at) and companies (api/v1/admin.py admin_delete_company) — the created_by/company_id FKs cannot be violated by any application code path; (c) `raise AlreadyApplied(...) from e` + CLI re-raise (tools/migrate_1c.py:225-227) — the chained traceback prints the original IntegrityError with the actual constraint name, so the root cause is never suppressed; (d) required_schema.py:381 makes ux_import_jobs_snapshot boot-mandatory, and a missing index produces no IntegrityError at all.
verdicts.repro_hint: To demonstrate the cosmetic mislabeling anyway (PG only, requires out-of-band DB surgery): pause apply between resolve_actor and db.flush() (e.g. breakpoint), run raw `DELETE FROM employees WHERE id = <actor>` in a second session (must first delete the actor's dependent rows or pick a fresh unreferenced employee), resume — flush raises ForeignKeyViolation, wrapped as AlreadyApplied; observe the traceback still prints the FK name via the __cause__ chain.

findings.title: Cutover ledger timestamps come from the untrusted operator process clock, not the DB clock the module itself declares authoritative
findings.claim: Freshness gating deliberately uses PostgreSQL clock_timestamp() because 'the operator machine is deliberately left without NTP and is untrusted' (freshness.py authoritative_now docstring). Yet apply.py:153 sets `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` from that same untrusted process clock and stamps it into the permanent ledger: StockMovement.created_at (t_close/t_open, apply.py:417,437), Inventory.updated_at, ImportJob.created_at/committed_at. The DB-clock value `_now2` obtained at apply.py:185 in the same transaction is available but unused for these timestamps.
findings.invariant: Rows written to the stock-movement ledger must carry timestamps from a trusted clock, so that CUTOVER_LEGACY_CLOSE/CUTOVER_OPENING_BALANCE order correctly against subsequent sales and land in the correct reporting day.
findings.attack_scenario: Operator laptop clock is 48h fast (the design explicitly assumes no NTP). Freshness passes (DB clock is correct), apply commits; the two cutover movements per (product,branch) are dated two days in the future. Sales recorded over the next two days are timestamped BEFORE the opening balance; daily movement reports and any chronological balance reconstruction misattribute the opening quantities, and the store-timezone report tests (known 'midnight trap') read them into the wrong day. Recoverable by rewriting created_at from the job trace, hence P2.
findings.evidence: apply.py:153 `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)  # vaqt QULFLARDAN KEYIN`; apply.py:417 `t_close, t_open = now, now + timedelta(microseconds=1)`; apply.py:437 `created_at=t_open if m["kind"]=="open" else t_close`; contrast freshness.py: process clock "AYNAN ishonchsiz mashina soatiga" — rejected for gating on PG.
findings.suggested_repro: Set the CLI machine clock +48h, run apply --commit on a staging clone; SELECT created_at FROM stock_movements WHERE ref_type='1c_cutover' — timestamps are in the future while column_mapping.freshness.now (DB clock) is correct.

verdicts.reasoning:
The core claim is provable by reading the code at 40150b5, and no protective mechanism covers it.

CONFIRMED MECHANICS (apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/apply.py, apply_migration/_execute):
- L153: `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` — process clock, taken after locks.
- L417: `t_close, t_open = now, now + timedelta(microseconds=1)`; L437: `StockMovement(created_at=t_open if m["kind"]=="open" else t_close)`; L444/448: `Inventory.updated_at = t_open`; L193: `ImportJob.created_at=now`; L217: `job.committed_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.
- The DB clock IS read in the same transaction (L142 `_now`, L185 `_now2` via freshness.authoritative_now → `SELECT clock_timestamp()`) but is used only for the freshness gate and the stored evidence blob (`column_mapping["freshness"]`), never for the ledger timestamps.
- apply_migration runs in the operator CLI process (apps/server/app/tools/migrate_1c.py, cmd_apply → `_session(read_only=False)` → direct DB connection), i.e. `datetime.now()` is exactly the machine freshness.py's authoritative_now docstring declares untrusted and deliberately NTP-less ("Jarayon soatiga TUSHILMAYDI — u ishonchsiz").

PROTECTIVE MECHANISMS HUNTED AND WHY EACH FAILS:
1. Model/DDL: apps/server/app/models/inventory.py L519+ — `StockMovement.created_at: DateTime(timezone=True)` has NO server_default, no trigger, no CHECK; the client-supplied value is stored verbatim (tables are built via create_all; db/schema.sql is documented in apply.py itself as never applied).
2. Freshness gate (freshness.assert_fresh): compares DB clock against the bundle's DECLARED `snapshot_at` only. The process clock never enters any comparison; `now` (L153) is never checked against `_now`/`_now2`. A skewed process clock passes the gate whenever the declared snapshot age is within [0, 24h] by the DB clock.
3. Partial accidental bound, which weakens only the literal 48h script: IF the bundle's snapshot_at was stamped by the same +48h machine, `SnapshotInFuture` (zero tolerance) rejects the apply. But snapshot_at is extractor-declared data (bundle.py; freshness.py docstring admits the code cannot verify it), so the defect remains fully reachable two ways: (a) bundle stamped on a correct-clock machine (1C server) + skewed CLI laptop → any skew passes; (b) same-machine skew smaller than the real snapshot→apply elapsed time (window up to 24h) → passes and stamps future-dated movements. The dangerous direction (opening balance dated AFTER subsequent sales) needs only a few hours of fast skew.
4. guard.assert_apply_allowed (guard.py): blocks production system_identifiers and APP_ENV=production at this SHA (Phase 5A). This limits current blast radius to staging/dev/rehearsal ledgers but is an explicitly temporary phase gate on the designated cutover path, not a clock protection; it does not touch timestamps.
5. verify_state / post-verify: reads back identity, prices, inventory — no timestamp check.

So the invariant ("ledger rows carry trusted-clock timestamps") is violated by construction: the trusted value `_now2` is on hand in the same transaction and discarded for stamping. Severity note: the literal 48h same-machine repro would actually be refused by SnapshotInFuture; the finding stands with the corrected exploit envelope (cross-machine clock split, or fast skew < elapsed snapshot age). P2 is consistent — recoverable from job trace, production currently gated.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Only partial/incidental ones: (1) freshness SnapshotInFuture zero-tolerance rejects the apply when the SAME skewed clock also stamped bundle.snapshot_at and the skew exceeds the real snapshot→apply elapsed time — bounding same-machine fast skew to under ~24h, but useless when the extractor machine's clock differs from the CLI machine's; (2) guard.assert_apply_allowed hard-blocks production DBs/envs at this SHA (Phase 5A), so mis-stamped ledgers are currently confined to staging/dev. Nothing (no server_default, trigger, CHECK, or comparison of process vs DB clock) protects the timestamps themselves.
verdicts.repro_hint: On an allowed staging clone (sysid in allowlist): produce the bundle on a correct-clock machine (snapshot_at = true now), then on the CLI machine set the clock +3h (not +48h — with a same-machine bundle that trips SnapshotInFuture) and run dry-run → plan → apply --commit. SELECT created_at FROM stock_movements WHERE ref_type='1c_cutover': rows are +3h in the future, while import_jobs.column_mapping->'freshness'->>'now' (DB clock) is correct. Variant proving the 48h case: keep bundle snapshot_at stamped by a correct clock, CLI clock +48h — freshness passes (declared age ~0) and movements land 48h in the future.

findings.title: Discovery bundle loader silently ignores unknown member files: they are not validated, not secret-scanned, and not covered by content_sha256
findings.claim: load_dir reads every file under the bundle directory into `members`, but load_members only parses the five REQUIRED_MEMBERS plus names matching `samples/*.json`; every other file (e.g. notes.md, export.json.bak, sample/x.json — note singular) is only size-checked and then dropped. redaction.scan (line 458) walks only the parsed structures, and canonical_projection/content_hash cover only the parsed members plus sample NAMES, so extra files are outside both the secret scan and the hash.
findings.invariant: The module's own contract is fail-closed whitelisting: an unknown JSON key rejects the whole bundle (invariant list, lines 13-21), and 'if a secret is found — REJECT'. An unknown member file should equally reject (or at minimum be hashed and scanned), otherwise `validate` prints ok and a content_sha256 that does not pin what is actually in the directory being archived and shared.
findings.attack_scenario: The sandbox operator zips the discovery folder that also contains a stray `1cv8-connection.txt` (with the infobase password) or a leftover raw export with customer data. `discovery_1c validate --dir` passes with ok=true and a clean content hash; the folder is then attached to the checklist and shared, leaking the secret that the redact layer exists to catch. Conversely, two directories with identical content_sha256 can differ in extra human-read files (a doctored summary-like extra .md), undermining the hash as an audit reference.
findings.evidence: bundle.py:449-455: `for name in sorted(members): if not name.startswith("samples/"): continue` — non-required, non-samples names fall through with no _need rejection; bundle.py:458-460 scan input is only `{"discovery":..., "metadata_sweep":..., "counts":..., "status":..., "summary_md":..., "samples": samples}`.
findings.suggested_repro: Add `password.txt` containing 'Pwd=secret123' to a valid bundle dir; `python -m app.tools.discovery_1c validate --dir <dir>` → ok:true, same content_sha256 as without the file.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding is accurate at SHA 40150b54; no protective mechanism exists anywhere on the validate path. Verified statically: (1) `load_dir` in apps/server/app/services/discovery_1c/bundle.py does `os.walk(path)` and reads EVERY file under the directory into `members` with no name filtering. (2) `load_members` performs exactly three checks on the member set: presence of the five REQUIRED_MEMBERS, a per-file `MAX_MEMBER_BYTES` size check over all members, and — only for names starting with `samples/` — a `.json`-suffix check plus parse/validate. Every other name (e.g. `password.txt`, `notes.md`, `export.json.bak`, `sample/x.json` singular) falls through the `if not name.startswith("samples/"): continue` loop and is silently dropped; there is no `_need(set(members) <= allowed, ...)` anywhere in the function. (3) The secret scan is `redaction.scan({"discovery":..., "metadata_sweep":..., "counts":..., "status":..., "summary_md":..., "samples": samples})` — and redact.py's `scan`/`_walk` (lines 65-79) walk only that parsed Python structure, never raw member bytes; so an unparsed extra file is never scanned. (4) `canonical_projection` includes only the parsed members plus `"samples": sorted(b.samples)` (sample NAMES), so `content_sha256` is byte-for-byte identical with or without the extra file. (5) The CLI (apps/server/app/tools/discovery_1c.py, `_validate`) just calls `load_dir` and prints `ok: True` + the hash — no additional directory-membership check, and no other module (epf_audit.py has no member/walk logic on this path) intervenes. This contradicts the module's own documented fail-closed contract (bundle.py header invariants; __init__.py: "Noma'lum kalit — RAD (whitelist)"), which is enforced for JSON keys via `_keys` but not for member file names. Attack path is concrete: a stray secret-bearing file in the bundle directory yields ok:true and an unchanged content hash; the hash also fails as an audit pin since two directories with different extra human-readable files hash identically. Severity assessment (P2, operational/leak risk rather than financial-ledger corruption) looks proportionate.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. The only checks touching unknown members are the MAX_MEMBER_BYTES size check (load_members, bundle.py) and, solely for the `samples/` prefix, a `.json`-suffix requirement. No whitelist rejection of unknown member names, no raw-byte secret scan, no inclusion of extra files in canonical_projection/content_hash, and no extra directory check in the CLI `_validate`.
verdicts.repro_hint: Not needed (statically provable), but: create a valid bundle via `python -m app.tools.discovery_1c synth --out D:/t`, record `validate --dir D:/t` output, then add `D:/t/password.txt` containing `Pwd=secret123` and rerun validate — it prints ok:true with the identical content_sha256, even though redact.py's patterns would flag `Pwd=` if the file were scanned.

findings.title: Migrator export imposes no length or control-character limits on product name/code/article — multi-megabyte or bidi/control-laden names pass validation into the catalog
findings.claim: bundle.py _validate only requires products[i].name to be a string or null (_opt_str), with the sole global bound being MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES=256MB; normalize.py _clean_text (line 241) merely strips edge whitespace — no length cap, no control-character/newline/RTL-override filtering. Product.name is an unbounded `String` column (apps/server/app/models/catalog.py:17), so on CREATE (or update_name with names=use_1c policy) a hostile export writes the value verbatim into products.name; verify_state compares equality so post-verify passes.
findings.invariant: Values imported by a bypass-the-API path should satisfy at least the constraints the normal catalog API enforces; catalog content served to POS/PWA/receipt renderers must be bounded and printable.
findings.attack_scenario: A tampered or malicious export.json (produced on the semi-trusted sandbox machine) contains 7000 products whose names are 5MB strings or contain U+202E/newline sequences. All bundle validation passes (names are strings, counts match), classify/mapping/apply succeed, and the catalog now bloats every /products sync payload and Electron/PWA render, and receipt lines can be visually spoofed via bidi controls. Recovery requires manual cleanup of the imported rows.
findings.evidence: bundle.py: `for k in ("guid","code","article","name","plu"): _opt_str(p,k,where)` — type check only; normalize.py:241-248 `_clean_text` returns `s.strip() or None` with no cap; git grep finds no length limit anywhere under services/migrator_1c; models/catalog.py:17 `name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String)` (no length → unbounded varchar on PG).
findings.suggested_repro: Build a minimal valid bundle whose single product has name='A'*5_000_000; verify-bundle, dry-run, plan, apply --rehearse on SQLite — no gate fires and the plan carries the full string as create.name.

verdicts.reasoning: The full path is provable by reading the code at 40150b54 and no protective mechanism exists. (1) apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/bundle.py _validate checks products[i].name only via _opt_str (type str-or-null); sole size bound is MAX_BUNDLE_BYTES=256MB in load_bytes, and the only character check is a lone-surrogate UTF-8 re-encode test — U+202E, newlines, and control chars pass. (2) normalize.py _clean_text is literally `t = str(raw).strip(); return t or None` — no length cap, no character filtering; the only name problem code in the package is MISSING_NAME. A grep of the whole migrator_1c tree for len()/truncation/isprintable/category confirms length checks exist only for barcodes (6-14), PLU (1-5), and hex tokens, never name/code/article. (3) mapping.py:518 puts r["name"] verbatim into create ops (and :499 into update_name under names=use_1c). (4) apply.py:347 constructs Product(name=c["name"]) directly via SQLAlchemy ORM and :384 sets p.name = update_name, bypassing the API's Pydantic layer entirely. (5) The invariant violation is concrete: the normal API enforces name max_length=300 (apps/server/app/schemas/catalog.py:75 ProductCreate; imports_v2.py:47 same cap), while products.name is unbounded `text NOT NULL` (db/schema.sql:209; models/catalog.py Product.name mapped_column(String) with no length, no CHECK). (6) verify_state (apply.py:491,496) compares equality, so the oversized/bidi value passes post-verify by construction. Refutation attempts failed: content_hash hashes but does not constrain the name; classify uses name only for MISSING_NAME and duplicate-name ambiguity; operator mapping review is procedural and blind to invisible bidi controls. The only partial backstop found: PostgreSQL rejects U+0000 in text columns, so a NUL-bearing name would abort apply with an error on PG — this covers neither length, U+202E, newlines, nor SQLite rehearsal, and is a crash, not a gate. Minor citation fix: at this SHA models/catalog.py:17 is Unit.name; Product.name is lower in the same file, equally unbounded.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: Only partial/incidental: PostgreSQL itself rejects U+0000 inside `text` values, so a NUL-containing name errors out at apply on PG (not on SQLite, and it is an unhandled failure, not a validation gate). Nothing constrains length, U+202E/bidi, newlines, or other control characters anywhere on the bundle->normalize->plan->apply path, and no DB CHECK or column length exists on products.name.
verdicts.repro_hint: Build a minimal valid binos-1c-v1 bundle (correct manifest counts, source_copy block, sidecar sha256) with one product whose name is 'A'*5_000_000 or contains '‮'/newlines; run verify-bundle, dry-run, plan (action CREATE, names policy irrelevant for create), then apply --rehearse on SQLite: no block/decide code fires except none, the plan op carries create.name verbatim, and post-verify passes with the full string stored in products.name.

findings.title: Unit dimension gate is an enumerated spelling list; unlisted gram/kilo spellings let an operator map mass->kg at the wrong magnitude (1200 g becomes 1200 kg)
findings.claim: check_unit_mapping (normalize.py:98) returns silently at line 114 ('if known is None: return') for any source unit name not in KNOWN_UNIT_DIMENSION (line 55). The mass section enumerates only specific spellings (г, гр, грамм, граммов, g, gr, gramm, gramma, ...). Common real-world variants such as 'граммы', 'грам', 'кило', English 'gram' are absent, so an operator --unit-map entry {'Граммы': 'kg'} passes the gate that was written precisely to reject gram->kg maps (its own comment: "aks holda 1000 g JIMGINA 1000 kg bo'lib yozilardi").
findings.invariant: A --unit-map entry whose source is a mass unit at a different magnitude than the BinOS target must be rejected (the migrator renames units, never converts quantities), so a gram-denominated 1C quantity can never be written as a kg quantity.
findings.attack_scenario: 1C base stores the unit as 'Граммы' (custom unit catalog entry). dry-run reports UNKNOWN_UNIT with that name; the operator, wanting to 'fix' it, supplies --unit-map '{"Граммы": "kg"}'. build_unit_table -> check_unit_mapping: norm key 'граммы' is not in KNOWN_UNIT_DIMENSION, so no dimension/magnitude claim is checked and the map is accepted. Every such row resolves unit_code='kg' (no UNKNOWN_UNIT, and no UNIT_DIFFERS when the LINK target or CREATE is kg). Stock '1200' (grams) flows unchanged through the plan into CUTOVER_OPENING_BALANCE movements and Inventory.qty as 1200 kg — a silent x1000 opening-balance corruption at cutover. Had the operator written the standard spelling 'грамм' the gate would have refused with the conversion-unsupported error; the unlisted spelling suppresses exactly that education.
findings.evidence: normalize.py:114 'if known is None:\n        return   # yangi nom o'rgatilmoqda — da'vo yo'q'. KNOWN_UNIT_DIMENSION mass keys (normalize.py:56-63) omit 'граммы'/'грам'/'кило'/'gram'. Once mapped, classify only checks membership in snap.units (classify.py:285-288) and code equality with the target (classify.py:429); nothing re-flags the mapping. The map is visible in report.unit_names_extra but no machine gate fires.
findings.suggested_repro: Unit-test: build_unit_table({'граммы': 'kg'}) succeeds while build_unit_table({'грамм': 'kg'}) raises ValueError; then run classify on a bundle row with unit name 'Граммы' and qty '1200' against a kg product and observe no UNKNOWN_UNIT/UNIT_DIFFERS code and stock_final 1200.

verdicts.reasoning: See above.
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None at machine level. The sole gate on unit-map semantics is check_unit_mapping's KNOWN_UNIT_DIMENSION lookup, which by design returns silently for unlisted source names; classify's UNKNOWN_UNIT (classify.py:287) and UNIT_DIFFERS (classify.py:429, mapping.py:386-394) test only the post-map BinOS code, and apply.py:157/344 merely replays classify with the reviewed report's unit_names_extra and checks the code exists in Units. The map is exposed for human review in report["unit_names_extra"], which is informational only.
verdicts.repro_hint: Pure unit test, no DB: from app.services.migrator_1c.normalize import build_unit_table — assert build_unit_table({"Граммы": "kg"}) returns a table containing {"граммы": "kg"} while build_unit_table({"грамм": "kg"}) raises ValueError. Then run classify on a bundle row with unit {"name": "Граммы"} and stock qty "1200" against a snapshot whose linked product has unit_code="kg" (or as a CREATE): assert neither UNKNOWN_UNIT nor UNIT_DIFFERS is in the row's codes and the planned opening stock is Decimal("1200").

verdicts.reasoning: (see above)
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None on the machine path. The only mechanisms are: (a) the enumerated KNOWN_UNIT_DIMENSION list itself (bypassed by any unlisted spelling); (b) report visibility — the map appears in report.unit_names_extra and the row's unit dict shows source/okei/binos, but no gate fires on it (human diligence only); (c) OKEI code is collected but never cross-checked against the mapped dimension — a missed opportunity, not a protection.
verdicts.repro_hint: Pure unit test, no PG needed for the gate half: assert build_unit_table({'Граммы': 'kg'})['граммы'] == 'kg' succeeds while pytest.raises(ValueError) for build_unit_table({'грамм': 'kg'}). Then normalize_product on a row with unit name 'Граммы', qty '1200' using that table: unit_code == 'kg', is_weighted True, stock_total Decimal('1200'), and no UNKNOWN_UNIT after classify against a snapshot where the target/CREATE unit is kg; confirm no UNIT_DIFFERS in n.decide. Same shape works for 'грам', 'кило', 'gram', 'kilo'.

findings.title: LINK never migrates the 1C scale PLU (or is_weighted) and no report code flags the divergence — weighted products linked to PLU-less BinOS rows become unsellable by scale label after cutover
findings.claim: In _build_plan, PLU is handled only for act=='CREATE' (mapping.py:472, plu=r['plu']) and REACTIVATE (mapping.py:484, clear-only). For LINK (including every automatic EXACT_MATCH) the 1C plu is discarded and apply's LINK branch (apply.py:364-390) writes only identity/price/name/barcodes — never plu_code or is_weighted. Classify's target-comparison codes (classify.py:418-444) cover NAME_DIFFERS, UNIT_DIFFERS, PRICE_CHANGES, barcode ownership and REACTIVATE_PLU_CONFLICT (deleted targets only); there is no PLU-mismatch or is_weighted-mismatch code for a live target, so the drop is invisible in the dry-run summary and template.
findings.invariant: Every material 1C field either migrates or produces an explicit decide/info code; nothing is silently dropped (the module's own stated rule: 'Hech narsa ... jimgina o'zgartirilmaydi').
findings.attack_scenario: CUTOVER_REFRESH: a BinOS product created earlier (e.g. Excel/v2 import) has plu_code NULL; the matching 1C row is weighted with plu '00537' and GUID identity -> EXACT_MATCH -> automatic LINK. Plan carries no PLU write; apply leaves plu_code NULL and is_weighted false. After cutover a scale label 2700537NNNNNC is scanned: POSKassa.tsx:498-515 parses every valid 27-prefixed EAN-13 FIRST and resolves only via products.find(p.is_weighted && pluMatches(p.plu_code, '00537')), with an explicit no-fallthrough error ('scaleNoProduct'). The product cannot be sold by scale label at all, and nothing in the migration report warned about it. With 452 scale PLUs live at Fayzan, any candidate-LINKed weighted item without a pre-existing BinOS PLU is affected.
findings.evidence: mapping.py:470-491 — PLU block starts 'if act == "CREATE":' with only an 'elif act == "REACTIVATE"' clear branch; ops entry for LINK contains no plu field. apply.py LINK path (else branch at apply.py:364) touches deleted_at/is_active/identity/prices/name only. classify.py step 5 (line 418 onward) has no PLU or is_weighted comparison for non-deleted targets.
findings.suggested_repro: classify a bundle row {guid matching product P, plu '00537', is_weighted true} where P has plu_code NULL: report row decide/info sets contain no PLU-related code; build_plan produces a LINK op without any plu key; after apply, P.plu_code is still NULL.

verdicts.reasoning: Every element of the claim is provable by reading the code at 40150b54. (1) apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/mapping.py, _build_plan step 6: `plu, clear_plu = None, False; if act == "CREATE": plu = r["plu"] ... elif act == "REACTIVATE" ...: clear_plu = True` — for LINK the 1C plu is never read, and the ops dict carries plu only inside `create` (CREATE) or as `clear_plu` (REACTIVATE); a LINK op has no PLU or is_weighted key at all. The end-of-plan PLU pass ("PLU rejaning O'ZI ichida") only iterates `o["create"]["plu"]` and REACTIVATE claims, so LINK is untouched there too. (2) apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/apply.py, _execute else-branch (LINK): writes only deleted_at check, is_active, identity (source_system/external_id), base_sell_price/base_buy_price, name, and barcodes — never plu_code or is_weighted; the post-apply verification (around lines 467-498) re-checks clear_plu and CREATE's plu_code/is_weighted but has no LINK PLU assertion, confirming no write was ever intended. (3) apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/classify.py step 5 (lines ~418-445): live-target comparison codes are exactly TARGET_LOT_TRACKED, NAME_DIFFERS, UNIT_DIFFERS, PRICE_CHANGES, PURCHASE_PRICE_CHANGES, EXTRA_BINOS_BARCODES, BARCODE_OWNED_BY_OTHER_PRODUCT, IDENTITY_CONFLICT; REACTIVATE_PLU_CONFLICT fires only under `if p["deleted"]`. There is no PLU-mismatch or is_weighted-mismatch code for a live target, and the summary counters (classify.py:582-583) count only PLU_COLLISION/REACTIVATE_PLU_CONFLICT/INVALID_PLU. Protective mechanisms I hunted for and ruled out: UNIT_DIFFERS (mapping.py:386-394) fires only when unit codes differ — a kg-unit target with NULL plu passes silently, and its only policies are block/skip_row (POLICY_CHOICES, mapping.py:38), never a fix; plu_collision policy applies only to CREATE/REACTIVATE; the raw report row does serialize both sides (row "plu"/"is_weighted" at classify.py:508 and candidate "plu_code"/"is_weighted" at classify.py:258), but EXACT_MATCH is the one automatic LINK (mapping.py docstring) requiring no operator decision, so nothing in the decide/info workflow or summary surfaces the drop. The downstream impact is also statically provable: packages/shared/src/screens/POSKassa.tsx onScan (~lines 498-515) parses a valid 27-prefix scale label FIRST, resolves only via `products.find(p => p.is_weighted && pluMatches(p.plu_code, scale.plu))`, and deliberately does NOT fall through to normal search (explicit `pos.scaleNoProduct` error), so a LINKed weighted product left with plu_code NULL (or is_weighted false) is unsellable by scale label. One mitigating nuance, not a refutation: the module's quoted rule (normalize.py:4 "Hech narsa ... jimgina o'zgartirilmaydi") is about not silently CHANGING values, and keeping the BinOS PLU may be a deliberate choice given the unreliable 1C PLU source (docs D27); but mapping.py's own docstring claims every gate — including PLU — is applied per selected target, and unlike name (NAME_DIFFERS + names policy) or price, PLU/is_weighted divergence on a live LINK target produces no code, no counter, and no decision point, so the operator cannot even see it. P2 severity is appropriate: it is a silent completeness gap, not corruption of working data (the target's scale sale was already broken pre-migration).
verdicts.protective_constraint_found: None. UNIT_DIFFERS (block/skip_row only, and only on unit-code inequality) and plu_collision (CREATE/REACTIVATE only) do not cover a same-unit live LINK target with NULL plu_code; apply.py's post-verify checks PLU only for CREATE and clear_plu; report rows contain both PLU values as raw data but no decide/info code, no summary counter, and EXACT_MATCH LINKs are automatic.
verdicts.repro_hint: Static proof suffices, but a one-assert test: build a bundle row {guid = product P's external_id, is_weighted: true, plu: "00537", unit кг} where P (live, unit kg) has plu_code NULL; classify → row primary EXACT_MATCH with decide/info sets containing no PLU/is_weighted code; build_plan → the LINK op dict has no key carrying "00537"; after apply, P.plu_code is still NULL and the run report shows zero PLU-related counters.

findings.title: Barcode GTIN equivalence covers only 12<->13 zero-padding; the 13<->14 (GTIN-14) padding of the same GTIN is treated as a different barcode, so one GTIN can end up on two products without quarantine
findings.claim: normalize_barcode (normalize.py:251-263) builds search_keys only for the 12-digit UPC-A <-> 13-digit '0'+UPC pair, and gtin_key (normalize.py:265-268) zero-pads only lengths 12 and 13. A 14-digit zero-padded form of an EAN-13 (valid per the 6-14 digit rule and standard GS1 GTIN-14 padding) is neither matched to the 13-digit owner in the catalog (barcode_owners via catalog.py barcode_keys uses the same search_keys) nor counted as an in-bundle collision, so both BARCODE_COLLISION_IN_BUNDLE and BARCODE_OWNED_BY_OTHER_PRODUCT stay silent and apply's DB re-check (apply.py:327-337, keyed by the same barcode_keys) also passes.
findings.invariant: Two representations of the same GTIN must be detected as the same barcode for collision quarantine, as the code already does for 12<->13 ('bitta GTIN').
findings.attack_scenario: BinOS product B owns barcode '4600000000001' (13-digit). The 1C export carries '04600000000001' (14-digit GTIN-14 padding of the same GTIN) on a different row that the operator CREATEs as product A. No decide code fires; apply inserts the 14-digit string on A. The catalog now holds the same GTIN under two products; whichever form a given scanner or import path emits determines which product a scan hits — a collision the quarantine was supposed to surface.
findings.evidence: normalize.py:257-260: only 'if len(v) == 12: k.add("0"+v)' and 'if len(v) == 13 and v.startswith("0"): k.add(v[1:])'. gtin_key: 'len(value) in (12, 13): return value.zfill(13)'. Validity range at :252 accepts 6-14 digits, so the 14-digit form is a legal, addable barcode.
findings.suggested_repro: gtin_key('04600000000001') != gtin_key('4600000000001') and barcode_keys('04600000000001') does not include the 13-digit form; classify a bundle with the 14-digit value against a catalog owning the 13-digit value and observe empty owners and no collision code.

verdicts.reasoning: The finding's citations are accurate at SHA 40150b5 and every layer of the quarantine chain reuses the same too-narrow equivalence, so no layer catches the 13<->14 pair. (1) apps/server/app/services/migrator_1c/normalize.py `normalize_barcode` accepts 6-14 digits as valid but builds search_keys variants only for len 12 (add "0"+v) and len 13 starting with "0" (add v[1:]); a 14-digit value gets search_keys=(v,) only, and `gtin_key` zero-pads only lengths 12/13, returning 14-digit values unchanged. Prepending '0' to an EAN-13 preserves the GS1 check digit (weights anchor at the right), so '0'+EAN-13 is a legal GTIN-14 of the same trade item — the exact analogue of the 12<->13 case the code already equates. (2) classify.py:303 keys bc_index by gtin_key, so the two forms land under different keys and BARCODE_COLLISION_IN_BUNDLE never fires. (3) catalog.py barcode_keys (187-190) returns search_keys and barcode_owners unions by_barcode_key over them, so the 14-digit form finds no owner when the catalog holds the 13-digit string; classify.py:438 BARCODE_OWNED_BY_OTHER_PRODUCT stays silent. (4) mapping.py (~446-466) computes others from those empty owners, so the value goes straight into barcodes_add with no policy prompt.
